The earlier ceremonies pointed towards Christ; the meal he establishes directs his people to the sacrifice that brings forgiveness.

The bread and wine are explained as symbols, not as a literal transformation into Jesus’ flesh and blood. The bread recalls his bodily life, perfect obedience and sacrificial death, while the cup points to his blood poured out for sinners. The message connects this sacrifice with forgiveness, changed hearts and the blessings of the new covenant. Jesus’ promise of drinking again in God’s kingdom also directs attention towards future fellowship with him.

The practical challenge is both personal and shared. Remembering the seriousness of sin and the mercy received should deepen gratitude rather than self-satisfaction. That gratitude is then expressed through loving the church. Sharing one bread declares that many believers belong to one body, not simply that separate individuals happen to worship in the same room. The Lord’s Table calls them to pursue unity, serve one another sacrificially and share a common commitment to proclaiming the gospel.

sermons.title: The Goodness of God | Wesam Saad
sermons.summary:
Against the weariness, illness, loss, and pressure experienced during the year, the sermon directs troubled hearts to meditate on the goodness of God. God’s goodness is presented not merely as moral correctness or usefulness, but as his pleasant beauty, tenderness, generosity, and faithfulness. It invites people to taste, see, enjoy, thank, and praise him. His goodness belongs to his very character and is displayed throughout creation, from the beauty of the world to his ongoing care for living creatures. God also gives ordinary gifts to all people and patiently extends the gospel invitation, showing kindness even to those who do not honour him.

The message then emphasises God’s particular goodness toward believers. He chose them according to his good pleasure and redeemed them at the cost of Christ’s precious blood, freely granting forgiveness, eternal life, adoption, freedom from sin, and fellowship with Christ. This goodness is inexhaustible and remains joined to God’s complete sovereignty. Trials therefore do not reveal a stronger or better refuge elsewhere. Believers are called to run to God as their good Shepherd, Father, physician, friend, and light; to remind themselves and one another of his character; and to find rest by delighting in him. Remembering God’s goodness produces gratitude, praise, confidence, and hope amid suffering.

sermons.title: The Pleasures Of The Resurrection
sermons.summary:
Can life beyond death be dismissed because it does not fit our experience of life now? In Mark 12:18–27, the Sadducees challenge Jesus with a marriage puzzle intended to discredit resurrection. His reply exposes a deeper problem: they have misunderstood both Scripture and God's power. Their apparently clever argument rests on assumptions that cannot define what God is able to do.

Jesus first corrects their picture of resurrection life. It is not simply earthly society continuing with the same marriage arrangements. The sermon encourages listeners to trust that life with God will be richer, not poorer, than the good relationships enjoyed here. Being like angels does not mean becoming angels; the hope centres on joyful fellowship with Christ and his people.

Jesus then turns to God's words to Moses about Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. God remains the God of his people beyond death, grounding hope in his living relationship with them. The message connects this assurance with Christ's death, resurrection and continuing love. Believers are encouraged to meditate on that hope and share it. Those who hesitate are invited to come to Jesus in their need, rather than trying to make themselves worthy first. Eternal life depends on the Saviour's power, not human self-repair.

sermons.title: The King and His Kingdom Will Stand
sermons.summary:
Human rebellion cannot overturn the reign of God’s appointed King. Psalm 2 confronts the nations’ resistance to the Lord and his anointed, then reveals a God whose purpose remains secure. The message traces the psalm through rebellion, God’s response, his declared plan and his invitation to take refuge in the Son.

Rebellion promises freedom while resisting the Creator’s rightful authority. Against that unrest, God is pictured as seated and unthreatened: neither human hostility nor the world’s turmoil can defeat his purpose. The New Testament’s use of the psalm identifies Jesus as the promised King, whose authority extends over the nations and whose judgement cannot be dismissed. Yet the closing appeal is also merciful. Those opposing him are called to wisdom, reverent worship and personal submission, finding safety in the very Son they have resisted.

For believers facing fear, suffering or uncertainty, Christ’s continuing reign provides confidence rather than a reason for passivity. The church is urged to make him known through the gospel, not to settle for improving outward behaviour while leaving people unreconciled to God. For those who have not trusted Christ, the invitation is urgent: abandon resistance, seek forgiveness and take refuge in him. His kingdom stands, and the proper response is both humble trust and faithful witness.

sermons.title: My Perfect Substitute
sermons.summary:
Barabbas walks free while the innocent Jesus is handed over to be crucified. This exchange provides a vivid picture of the substitution at the heart of the gospel: Christ bears what guilty sinners deserve so that those who trust him may receive forgiveness and righteousness. The sermon asks how God can remain just while justifying the ungodly, and locates the answer in the willing sacrifice of his Son.

The trial also exposes competing forms of self-interest. The religious leaders act from envy, the crowd demands its preferred outcome, and Pilate protects his position by yielding to pressure despite recognising Jesus’ innocence. Against that background, Christ’s meekness stands out. He accepts suffering without retaliating, and the guilty prisoner receives freedom he could not secure by claiming innocence. The account does not reveal whether Barabbas later believed; his release serves as an illustration, not proof of his spiritual salvation.

Listeners are invited to recognise their own need for this substitute and place their confidence personally in Jesus. For believers, the exchange should produce astonishment, gratitude and willing devotion. Christ’s love calls for more than a reserved portion of life. Work, family relationships and daily desires are to become opportunities to honour the one who gave himself for them.

sermons.title: Legalism and Mysticism
sermons.summary:
Colossians 2:16–19 warns the church about two ways false teaching draws people away from the sufficiency of Christ. Legalism says that acceptance with God and spiritual growth depend on human achievement, religious rules or external observances. It judges Christians over food, festivals and other matters that are shadows rather than substance. Paul does not forbid choices in matters where Scripture is silent, but he refuses to let anyone bind another believer’s conscience. Christian freedom is not permission for self-centred living; choices should still be made according to whether they honour Christ and draw the believer nearer to him.

Mysticism substitutes private visions, spiritual experiences and impressive displays of humility for confidence in Christ and his word. Such claims can inflate people with pride, grant them false authority and place others under their control. Paul directs believers instead to hold fast to Christ, the head who supplies and grows his whole body. The sermon urges the church to test its own heart, reject both self-righteous effort and unverifiable spiritual claims, and cling to Jesus alone. He has forgiven sin, defeated the enemy and provides everything necessary for growth through his Spirit, his word and his care for the church. The path forward is faithful obedience flowing from completeness in Christ.

sermons.title: The Christ Centred Husband
sermons.summary:
What does a Christ-centred husband look like behind closed doors? This sermon on 1 Peter 3:7 challenges the idea that leadership means demanding service, asserting superiority or withdrawing into private interests. The preacher places marriage under Christ’s example: the one who loved his church and gave himself for her. A husband’s conduct at home is presented as part of his witness, not a private exception to Christian discipleship.

The verse is developed through understanding, cherishing and honouring one’s wife. Understanding requires time, attentive listening and genuine knowledge of her concerns, strengths and fears. Shared residence or participation in church life cannot replace personal involvement. Care is to be patient and tender, not aggressive, controlling or dismissive. The sermon also stresses a wife’s dignity as a fellow heir of grace, while maintaining the duty of loving treatment where a spouse is not a believer.

The warning about hindered prayers connects daily conduct with spiritual fellowship. Husbands are urged to pray with and for their wives, examine distractions and show respect in both private and public speech. Young men are encouraged to develop these habits before marriage. The closing invitation turns to Christ as the bridegroom and calls those who do not know him to trust his finished work.

sermons.title: The Great Deception
sermons.summary:
Jesus' warning against deception calls for more than curiosity about the end times. Focusing on Mark 13:5–6, the preacher explores the command to remain alert, the rise of false Christs and the deception associated with the Antichrist. He understands these warnings within a future tribulation, while emphasising their present purpose: God's people must follow the true Christ rather than treat prophecy as entertainment or a display of theological knowledge.

The sermon distinguishes ordinary false teaching from claims to be Christ himself. Impressive signs, attractive promises and persuasive appearances are not treated as proof of truth. The preacher then contrasts the Antichrist's lawlessness and demand for worship with Jesus' obedient humanity, genuine divinity and saving power. Christ does not merely offer temporary relief from worldly problems; his death and resurrection provide forgiveness that a counterfeit deliverer cannot give.

The practical response is close attention and allegiance to Jesus. Trials can become occasions to surrender competing attachments, while correction from another believer can expose the need for his cleansing and strength. Rather than defending sin, listeners are urged to draw nearer to the Saviour. The message also warns against postponing faith until deception becomes stronger, and invites those who do not yet know Christ to receive the salvation he freely offers now.

sermons.title: Transcendence and Immanence | Knowing the Unknown God
sermons.summary:
God’s transcendence and immanence belong together, giving a view of the God Scripture reveals. Transcendence means that God is infinitely exalted above and distinct from creation. He is not part of the universe or dependent upon it, but its Creator, sovereign Ruler, and sustaining Lord. His majesty does not fade like human greatness, and his thoughts encompass what people cannot see. This truth calls for reverence, frees believers from the fear of people, and encourages trust when God’s purposes are difficult to understand. His ways remain perfect even when the future is hidden from us.

Immanence means that this exalted God is also present and active within his world. His power governs creation, his authority extends everywhere, and his knowledge reaches every visible action and hidden thought. Yet God draws especially near to his people. The Son became human as Emmanuel, suffered, died, and rose so that those he saves could enjoy fellowship with him. By his Spirit, God dwells in believers and meets them with love, peace, joy, strength, and companionship. The sermon urges Christians facing guilt, loneliness, or heavy trials to remember that the sovereign God has not abandoned them. Because he is both above all things and lovingly near, they can bring anxieties to him, rest in his care, and approach his throne of grace through Christ.

sermons.title: Israel Under Attack
sermons.summary:
Jesus’s warning in Mark 13:14–23 combines urgent action with assurance of God’s care. The preacher understands the abomination of desolation as a future desecration that brings severe danger to those in Judea. The command to flee leaves no room for delaying over possessions, even things that ordinarily seem essential.

The passage also recognises the vulnerability of those for whom escape will be especially difficult. Jesus’s concern for pregnant women and nursing mothers, and his instruction to pray about the conditions of flight, reveal compassion within a sobering warning.

Danger does not mean God has abandoned his people. The sermon emphasises his decision to limit the days for the sake of his elect. It distinguishes physical survival in this setting from salvation through faith in Christ, which persecution cannot prevent. False claims and impressive signs must not displace confidence in what Jesus has already said.

The practical response is watchful perseverance, strengthened through fellowship. Believers are encouraged to speak of Christ’s faithfulness, remind one another of his promises and pray together instead of relying on possessions or distracting debate. The invitation reaches into our present circumstances: seek refuge in Christ, comfort others with his Word and let the hope of his return shape decisions that count beyond this life.

sermons.title: God's Matchless Mercy | Knowing the Unknown God
sermons.summary:
God’s mercy is presented as his compassionate response to sinful, hurting people. The sermon begins with the mercy seat in Israel’s sanctuary, showing that guilty people approach the holy Judge by relying on mercy rather than merit. God displays a general mercy toward all creation: he patiently withholds deserved judgment, provides life and goodness, and calls people to repent. Scripture’s story shows this patience, from the years before the flood to Jesus grieving over Jerusalem and praying for those who crucified him. Yet this patience must not be mistaken for permission to continue in sin, because the opportunity to receive mercy in this life will not last forever.

The sermon then describes God’s saving mercy toward those who come to Christ. It is sovereign, undeserved, abundant, tender, and everlasting. God saves not because he discovers righteousness in a person, but because his heart is merciful. Paul’s conversion illustrates compassion reaching a violent persecutor, while the father welcoming the prodigal son portrays God’s readiness to receive his returning children. Even loving discipline serves restoration rather than rejection. Because God’s mercy is greater than human sin, believers can return to him honestly instead of hiding in shame. The message invites every listener to abandon self-reliance, trust Jesus, and ask God for the forgiveness and cleansing that flow from his inexhaustible mercy.

sermons.title: Earthquakes, Famines And Pestilence
sermons.summary:
What can Jesus' warning about earthquakes and famines reveal about God himself? Beginning with Mark 13:8, the preacher moves beyond the scale of coming disasters to consider the character of the God who rules over them. He understands the passage as describing intensifying events before Christ's return and reads it alongside Ezekiel and Revelation. The central concern is not simply what will happen, but what these events disclose about divine sovereignty, wrath and mercy.

The sermon stresses that destructive powers do not operate independently of God. Their authority is granted and bounded; the Lamb remains in control rather than watching helplessly. At the same time, judgment reveals God's settled opposition to evil. The seriousness of sin is not softened, and the predicted terror challenges any comfortable view of rebellion against him.

Yet the message concludes with mercy rather than devastation alone. The preacher interprets the response of earthquake survivors in Revelation as evidence of God awakening people to repentance, and connects their response with the Spirit opening their eyes to Christ. Salvation is presented as freely given because of God's compassion, not earned by the worthiness of those who call on him. The closing prayer asks for that awakening now, inviting listeners to recognise their need for Christ without waiting for catastrophe.

sermons.title: Is Jesus Willing to Make Me Clean?
sermons.summary:
A man covered with leprosy comes to Jesus with a simple appeal: if Jesus is willing, he can make him clean. Exploring this encounter in Luke 5, the sermon presents the healing as an illustration of salvation. Its three movements consider the ugliness of sin, the sinner’s plea and the Saviour’s response. The aim is to awaken gratitude for grace and a desire to tell others about Christ.

The preacher uses the man’s uncleanness and exclusion to illustrate the helplessness and separation associated with sin. The man approaches without credentials or a claim to deserve healing, yet with confidence in Jesus’ power. His request for cleansing is understood as pointing beyond outward relief towards restored fellowship with God.

Jesus’ touch and willing response receive particular attention. The sermon distinguishes believing that Christ has power from trusting his compassion towards the undeserving. Listeners troubled by repeated failures are directed to his welcome and to the cross as evidence of his mercy. The immediate cleansing then displays his authority. Finally, the instruction to appear before the priest shows respect for the law and makes the restored man a testimony to Jesus’ identity. Believers are encouraged to remember their own dependence on grace and speak of the Saviour who received them.

sermons.title: Behold! The EXALTED Christ
sermons.summary:
Christ’s humiliation does not end in defeat. Having willingly served and obeyed the Father even through death, Jesus is raised and exalted above every authority. His resurrection and ascension give believers confidence that suffering and lowly service will not have the final word. The risen Saviour remains truly human, intercedes for his people and will bring them into the glory of his presence.

The Father’s exaltation of Jesus also calls every creature to recognise his lordship. No person is exempt from bowing before him or acknowledging who he is. Yet this universal recognition is not presented as universal salvation. Believers will worship with grateful affection, while those who reject him will acknowledge his authority in judgment. The urgent invitation is to trust the crucified and risen Christ now, rather than continue resisting his call.

For Christians, honouring this exalted Lord takes a practical shape in everyday relationships. His example challenges selfish ambition, the pursuit of personal recognition and the expectation of always being served. Looking to the interests of others, serving fellow believers and working for church unity bring glory to the Father. Hope of life with Christ should encourage faithful use of the present, not passive waiting or wasted opportunities to love.

sermons.title: Praising Him With All She Could
sermons.summary:
Mary’s costly anointing of Jesus looks wasteful to the disciples, but Jesus calls it a good deed. Mark 14:4–9 invites us to reconsider the value we place on devotion to Christ. Judas calculates the perfume’s price while concealing greed beneath concern for the poor, and the disciples join his harsh criticism of Mary.

Jesus defends her and explains the opportunity she has recognised. Care for the poor remains important, but his approaching death gives this moment a particular urgency. Mary’s worship takes priority, and her anointing anticipates his burial. Service for Christ must flow from love for him rather than crowding out attention to him.

Her gift also expresses trust, willing generosity and sacrificial affection. She does not bargain with Jesus or offer only what costs her nothing. His own self-giving love provides the reason for wholehearted devotion in return.

The application is not a command for every believer to transfer all their money to the church. Nor is love measured by the size of a donation. The sermon asks what our use of money, time and effort reveals about our trust and priorities. Mary challenges us to honour Christ cheerfully, value his approval above criticism and grow beyond giving merely enough to preserve our comfort.

sermons.title: Longing For God in Afflictions
sermons.summary:
Psalm 42 gives honest language for a believer who feels spiritually dry, overwhelmed, and distant from God. The psalmist weeps, remembers former worship, hears enemies question God’s presence, and describes affliction as waves rolling over him. He knows that God remains sovereign, yet he cannot presently experience the joy and nearness he once knew. The sermon uses this struggle to remind believers of human frailty and their continuing need for God. It also urges the church to respond gently to suffering brothers and sisters rather than offering impatient answers or treating their distress as weakness.

The psalmist’s response begins with thirst for the living God. Like a deer seeking water, he continues to seek God rather than looking to earthly distractions for lasting satisfaction. He remembers worship with God’s people, recalls the Lord’s covenant love, and speaks truth to his own troubled soul: hope in God, for he will praise him again. This is not denial of pain or merely positive thinking; it is choosing God’s promises over the conclusions suggested by changing feelings. The sermon calls believers to seek Christ diligently, remain in fellowship, remember the cross and God’s enduring love, and rehearse the hope of resurrection and Christ’s return. Even when relief is not immediate, dependable hope in God can sustain the soul through darkness.

sermons.title: Bless Yahweh
sermons.summary:
Psalm 103 calls the whole person to bless the Lord and remember his benefits. David does not wait for an external stimulus to create worship; he addresses his own soul and summons every thought, affection and faculty to praise God’s holy name. This wholehearted worship grows from contemplating who God is—compassionate, gracious, patient, faithful and sovereign—and from refusing the spiritual forgetfulness that lets his goodness slip from view.

The opening verses name five benefits. God pardons every iniquity, removing guilt through Christ’s saving work. He heals the diseases of the soul, giving new sight, desires and strength to follow him. He redeems life from destruction, freeing his people from condemnation. He crowns them with steadfast love and compassion, remaining faithful and meeting their pain with a father’s tenderness. Finally, he satisfies them with good things, above all with lasting fellowship in Christ.

These gifts show that God does not perform an incomplete rescue. He forgives, restores, preserves and satisfies his people, and each benefit gives another reason for sincere praise. Believers are encouraged to preach these truths to their own souls so gratitude shapes their words and lives. Those seeking satisfaction in passing pleasures are called instead to trust Jesus, in whom the sermon locates forgiveness, healing, redemption and enduring life.

sermons.title: Jesus Might Come Back Today!
sermons.summary:
Studying Christ’s return should change how we live, not merely enlarge our knowledge of future events. In Mark 13:32–37, Jesus closes his teaching with a repeated command to remain alert. Because we do not know the appointed time, our response should be readiness rather than attempts to calculate a date.

The picture of a master leaving servants with assigned tasks brings that readiness into everyday life. Our abilities, possessions and opportunities have been entrusted to us for Christ’s service. Like a doorkeeper watching for the master, we are called to work faithfully while eagerly anticipating his return.

Spiritual sleep is not ordinary physical rest. It is complacency: allowing worldly pleasure, anxiety or self-absorption to displace affection for Jesus. Expecting him to return renews endurance, restores joy to service and helps us choose what matters. Practical care for another believer can then become an expression of devotion rather than an inconvenient interruption.

Wholehearted service rests on the worth of the Saviour, not confidence in our own worthiness. His blood answers the guilt that might otherwise keep us from serving. For those who have not trusted him, readiness begins with coming to Christ now. He alone can forgive and change us; neither religious knowledge nor our own moral improvement can save.

sermons.title: Desiring True Blessings Within God's Law
sermons.summary:
Psalm 119:1–8 answers the search for lasting happiness by directing people to God, the source of blessing. The psalmist first looks at those whose lives are shaped by God’s Word. They walk in his ways, treasure his testimony, seek him wholeheartedly, and refuse to make peace with sin. This blamelessness is not sinless perfection. Believers fall, but they repent, rise again, and continue pursuing Christ because they find greater pleasure in him than in disobedience. True happiness therefore rests neither in money nor possessions, but in communion with God and a life ordered by his truth.

The psalmist then looks toward heaven and recognises that God has commanded his precepts to be kept diligently. Grace does not change what is holy; through Christ it changes the believer’s relationship to God’s law. Christ has borne condemnation and supplied righteousness, so the law becomes a friend and guide rather than a condemning master. Finally, the psalmist looks at himself and prays that his ways will be established. He longs for holiness, assurance, gratitude, and dependence upon grace. The sermon calls Christians to examine whether they are growing, confess wandering desires, seek God with their whole heart, and pray for strength to obey. Diligent walking fosters assurance, while reliance on God guards against self-confidence and keeps believers pressing toward him.

sermons.title: Beggars, Bound, Blind, and Bruised - Part 1
sermons.summary:
This first message on Jesus in the Nazareth synagogue opens the narrative of Luke 4:14–30 but concentrates on verses 14–21. The preacher follows Jesus as he returns to Galilee in the Spirit’s power and teaches in synagogues, then reads from Isaiah in the place where he grew up. He emphasizes that teaching God’s word is central to Jesus’ ministry. The initially favourable response to Jesus is not treated as the same thing as trusting him; the preacher asks listeners whether their admiration becomes genuine devotion.

Jesus reads a promise of good news to the poor, release for captives, sight for the blind and freedom for the oppressed, then announces that the Scripture is fulfilled in their hearing. The sermon interprets these images as a picture of human spiritual need and of the rescue Jesus offers. The poor cannot provide their own righteousness, captives need release, the blind need sight, and the oppressed need relief. The announced favourable year is presented as a time of forgiveness and freedom. Listeners are invited to recognise their need and turn to Christ rather than merely observe the scene from a distance. Believers are encouraged that Jesus came for needy people and urged to remain humble, since their dependence on him does not end when they first believe.

sermons.title: The Secret to Christian Contentment
sermons.summary:
From Philippians 4:11–13, this sermon explains that Christian contentment is learned through changing circumstances rather than produced by possessions, comfort, or favourable relationships. Money, homes, careers, cars, food, and even loved ones cannot bear the weight of being a lasting source of satisfaction. Their appeal changes, problems arise, and people disappoint. Paul instead learns to be content in every circumstance because Jesus is the settled peace of his soul. This learning occurs in God’s school of testing, where believers discover through experience that his providence remains wise in both large and ordinary details.

Paul knows how to live with little or much, to be hungry or well supplied, without allowing either condition to determine his joy. His trials are not interruptions to contentment but the means through which God teaches it. The familiar words “I can do all things through him who strengthens me” therefore do not promise success in every chosen ambition. In context, they mean that Christ supplies strength to fulfil God-given duties faithfully and remain content within the circumstances God assigns. The sermon urges believers to deepen their relationship with Christ, reject the repeated promise that one more possession will satisfy, receive each trial as instruction, and depend on Jesus for grateful endurance.

sermons.title: Behold the Excellency of Jesus Christ
sermons.summary:
The arrest of Jesus reveals a Saviour whose character remains beautiful under the harshest pressure. Judas arrives with an armed crowd, betrays him with a kiss, and the disciples eventually flee. Against that background, the message draws attention to three qualities of Christ: his forbearance towards enemies, his fearlessness before danger and his faithfulness to those who belong to him.

Jesus meets Judas’s betrayal without bitterness or retaliation. His patient appeal shows a readiness to receive sinners who genuinely seek forgiveness. Peter’s impulsive use of a sword provides a sharp contrast to Jesus’ calm trust in the Father. Jesus does not need to hide or resist arrest to demonstrate courage; he openly challenges the manner of his capture and willingly advances towards the suffering ahead. Even then, his concern reaches beyond himself as he seeks the safety of his disciples.

The message invites listeners to find refuge in this patient, courageous and faithful Saviour. His love is presented not as permission to persist in sin, but as the kindness that breaks self-confidence and draws people to repentance. Believers are urged to keep considering Christ’s character, especially when fellowship becomes difficult or criticism provokes defensiveness. Receiving his mercy should shape a gracious response to others rather than anger and resentment.

sermons.title: Grace That Gives Beyond Expectations | Luke 1v56 66
sermons.summary:
The birth and naming of John in Luke 1:56–66 display grace that gives beyond expectation. Grace is God’s unearned gift to people who deserve the opposite, not mere leniency or a reward for improvement. It arrives according to God’s time and is not defeated by long delay, human impossibility, or spiritual barrenness. Elizabeth’s unexpected son turns public shame into honour, while the name John—“Yahweh is gracious”—announces that God’s purpose outranks family custom and inherited identity.

Zechariah’s obedience in naming the child is followed by restored speech and eruptive praise. The surrounding community moves from gossip and judgment to holy awe, and news of God’s mercy spreads through the countryside. Grace therefore cannot be hoarded: when it truly changes a person, it produces gratitude, worship, freedom from man-made traditions, and an outward effect on other believers. Yet John is not the final subject. His life and name point to Jesus Christ, the Lamb of God who brings grace upon grace. The sermon urges believers to recognise the greater grace they have received in Christ, let it reshape everyday identity and decisions, speak of him openly, and live as grateful followers rather than returning to cultural restrictions, habitual sin, or a sense of entitlement.

sermons.title: Loving Others
sermons.summary:
Loving a neighbour is not a bargain in which care is offered only when it is returned. Focusing on Mark 12:31, the sermon explores the command to love others as ourselves and connects it with wholehearted love for God. The two commands are not competing demands on a limited supply of affection. God is the source from whom believers receive; their neighbours are people towards whom that received love can overflow.

The message describes love for God as dependence on his sufficiency and love for others as generous service. A neighbour is not simply someone attractive, agreeable or useful, but the person encountered in ordinary life. Different relationships require different expressions of care, yet love should not be conditional on getting something back. The intensity of our concern for ourselves becomes a challenge to take another person's needs and salvation seriously.

Practical applications reach into family life and church membership: being present, praying, teaching, giving time and serving rather than merely consuming. The strength for such love is found in Christ. His cross demonstrates God's undeserved love, giving believers confidence to draw near despite their failures. Obedience also brings deeper fellowship with Jesus. Rather than waiting to be treated better, listeners are urged to serve from the security and joy they receive in him.

sermons.title: The Christ-Centered Parents
sermons.summary:
From Colossians 3:21, this sermon calls fathers and mothers to exercise parental authority without provoking their children to discouragement. Parents remain responsible for discipline, instruction, and protection; the command does not require surrendering authority whenever a child dislikes a boundary. Nor is every discouraged feeling caused by parental failure, since children face many trials and bear responsibility for their own choices. The question is whether a parent’s own conduct unnecessarily irritates a child, weakens motivation to obey, or makes the home an obstacle to faithful growth.

The sermon identifies five ways parents may exasperate their children. Excessive strictness can make personal fear, laziness, or preference into unnecessary rules. The opposite error, refusing clear standards and diligent discipline, leaves children confused and insecure. Neglect communicates that work, money, or other activity matters more than being present to guide them. Constant criticism without affection or encouragement drains confidence. Most seriously, parents may provide education, comfort, and morality while failing to lead their children toward Jesus Christ. The message urges parents to choose battles wisely, maintain biblical standards, give time and tender encouragement, and speak about Christ throughout ordinary family life. Rather than parenting for convenience or approval, they should model the Saviour’s compassion and make love for God the central lesson of the home.

sermons.title: Follow Godly Examples
sermons.summary:
Philippians 3:17 calls believers to join in following Paul’s example and to watch those who live according to the same pattern. Christian growth is not a solitary project. God brings his people into the church, where they receive encouragement, correction, practical wisdom, and living examples of faith. Mature believers are called to keep growing and pass what they learn to others, while others must seek models. Discipleship crosses age, ethnicity, personality, and shared interests because Christ binds the church together. Unembodied, unshared knowledge does not fulfil this calling.

Paul does not present himself as perfect or draw attention to his personality. He can say “follow me” because his life is being shaped by Christ. His pressing toward holiness, prayer, gratitude, concern for the church, endurance under hardship, gospel courage, humility, and joy provide patterns others can practise. Scripture similarly calls church leaders to be examples, but Paul also directs attention to other believers whose conduct reflects the same apostolic pattern. Each Christian remains responsible to observe, imitate, and grow; no mentor can obey on another person’s behalf. The sermon therefore asks whom we are following and whom we are influencing. Believers should seek people whose character displays Jesus, learn from them attentively, and become examples who help the next person pursue holiness and maturity in Christ.

sermons.title: Behold! The Agony Of Christ
sermons.summary:
Gethsemane reveals the heart of Jesus in the face of profound suffering. Following Mark 14:32–36, the message considers him as a sympathetic Saviour, a suffering servant and a submissive Son. His anguish is not treated as a reason to turn away, but as an invitation to see more deeply the love and obedience of the one who came to save sinners.

Jesus brings imperfect disciples close even when their self-confidence and repeated failures are evident. His patience offers comfort to believers conscious of their own weakness. The sermon then considers the cup before him: the burden of human sin and the judgment it deserves. His distress is presented as more than fear of physical pain or rejection. He willingly bears what sinners could not bear for themselves, opening the way to forgiveness and eternal life.

In prayer, Jesus acknowledges both the Father’s loving care and his sovereign power. He expresses his anguish honestly while surrendering himself to the Father’s will. The response urged is grateful worship that becomes a changed way of living: relinquishing self-confidence, showing compassion, serving sacrificially and trusting God through difficulty. Those who do not yet know Christ are called to bring their sins to this gracious Saviour rather than rely on their own goodness.

sermons.title: Satisfied in Him
sermons.summary:
Drawing from Psalm 63:1–2, this sermon presents the human soul as possessing a hunger no created pleasure can finally satisfy. God placed that longing within people so they would seek him, yet relationships, possessions, entertainment, work, and comfort repeatedly compete for its direction. David models a healthier response while fleeing into the wilderness after betrayal by his son Absalom. Stripped of position, security, and familiar support, he does not seek God merely as a means to recover his kingdom. He seeks God himself as refuge, comfort, and the supreme satisfaction of his soul.

David’s pursuit is earnest and desperate, like a thirsty traveller who knows that water is a matter of life and death. His longing leads him to meditate on God’s power and glory in the sanctuary. Believers reflect on that power through Christ’s cross, where Jesus bore sin and judgment and accomplished redemption. Such meditation does not guarantee that earthly problems will disappear. It anchors the heart in the One who can sustain his people through the trial and fill them with joy that circumstances cannot explain. The sermon urges Christians to stop treating created gifts as replacements for God, run to him first when hardship arrives, contemplate his saving power, and receive trials as opportunities to deepen their dependence and display his goodness.

sermons.title: Christ, Our Hope in Suffering
sermons.summary:
First Peter 2 presents Christ as the model and hope for Christians who suffer unjustly. Believers should not be surprised by mistreatment, because Jesus warned that his followers would face persecution. Peter directs them to the sinless Christ, who endured the cross without reviling his attackers or threatening revenge. Instead, Jesus entrusted himself to the Father who judges righteously. His response was not weakness or passivity; he was fulfilling the Father’s will and redeeming his people. Christ bore their sins so that they could die to sin, live to righteousness, and return to the shepherd and guardian of their souls.

The sermon calls Christians to trace the pattern of Jesus’ life. When insulted or treated unfairly, they should resist retaliation, speak truth with kindness, entrust justice to God and remember that they needed mercy. Following Christ does not mean reproducing his atoning work, nor does it require perfect strength. The Holy Spirit helps believers walk in the footsteps of their shepherd, whose presence is near in suffering. Remembering and preaching the gospel to themselves warms the heart and gives strength for humble obedience. By looking to the cross, Christians can forgive, put sin to death, live faithfully and even rejoice that they have been counted worthy to suffer for Jesus’ name.

sermons.title: Scripture Alone Produces Blessings
sermons.summary:
Psalm 119 opens by declaring the blessing of those whose way is blameless, who walk in the Lord’s instruction, keep His testimonies, and seek Him wholeheartedly. The sermon asks where people look for joy, purpose, and meaning. Homes, possessions, work, family, and personal achievements cannot supply an enduring blessing. Scripture, breathed out by God and worth the sacrifices made to preserve and translate it, directs believers to the living God and provides truth, comfort, hope, wisdom, strength, and the path of holy living.

This blessing does not mean that obedience earns salvation or produces sinless perfection. God’s perfect law exposes human sin and drives people to Christ, who fulfilled the law and redeems those under it. For those made new by grace, obedience becomes the grateful direction of life. They guard God’s testimony, seek Him with heart and mind, and desire to walk His way. Reading Scripture is not merely accumulating information or locating isolated rules. Its purpose is to find and know Jesus, deepen delight in Him, and live accordingly. The sermon therefore challenges believers to read, meditate on, believe, pray through, and obey the Bible, using ordinary opportunities at home, while travelling, and with children. Those outside Christ are invited to begin with poverty of spirit, mourn their sin, and take refuge in the Son who forgives.

sermons.title: What Would Simeon Do?
sermons.summary:
In Luke's account of Simeon meeting the infant Jesus, the preacher sees another witness to the promised Christ. Simeon is introduced without an important public office, yet he is righteous and devout, waiting for Israel's consolation and guided by the Holy Spirit. The preacher holds up his character, longing, reception of Jesus and prayer as a pattern worth considering. He explains Simeon's righteousness as received through faith rather than earned by a tally of good deeds, and his devotion as an active hunger for God. The Spirit's promise that Simeon would see the Christ gives his waiting a clear focus.

When Jesus is brought into the temple, Simeon takes him into his arms and blesses God. He can speak of departing in peace because, in the preacher's reading, he has seen God's salvation in the person of Jesus. Simeon's prayer looks beyond himself to light for Gentiles and glory for Israel. The sermon therefore calls listeners not merely to admire Jesus from a distance but to receive and treasure him. It also challenges the assumption that usefulness to God depends on worldly status. Like this otherwise little-known man, believers are urged to long for Christ, remain faithful in ordinary life and find peace in him even when facing loss and death.

sermons.title: The Commissioning of The Son of God
sermons.summary:
Preaching from Luke 3:21–22, the speaker invites listeners to consider Jesus' baptism as the beginning of his public mission. He emphasizes the surprising humility of the sinless Son standing among people who came confessing sins. Jesus did not need repentance himself. The preacher gives two reasons for his baptism: he identifies with the people he came to save, and he undertakes the obedient life they could not live. He connects that obedience with Christ's righteousness as well as his bearing of sin, urging believers to approach God on Christ's merit rather than waiting until they feel worthy.

The sermon then follows the scene as Jesus prays, the Holy Spirit descends, and the Father speaks. The preacher describes Jesus in his human life as dependent on the Spirit and calls believers to rely on the Spirit too. He stresses that the Spirit's descent is described as being like a dove, not that the Spirit is literally a bird. The Father's words, calling Jesus his beloved Son and expressing pleasure in him, reveal a love that did not begin with this event. The speaker invites believers to delight in the Son whom the Father loves and offers unbelieving listeners a direct appeal to receive him. Throughout, his aim is to direct attention to Jesus' humility, dependence and belovedness.

sermons.title: Impossible to Believe
sermons.summary:
Drawing on Jesus’ encounter with the rich young ruler in Mark 10, this sermon asks why saving faith is not merely hard but impossible for people to produce by themselves. The ruler wanted eternal life as an addition to the security he already enjoyed, not as a surrender of everything that competed with Christ. His response exposes two false approaches: trying to earn acceptance through religious effort, and treating belief as bare mental agreement that leaves worldly ambitions untouched. Wealth receives particular attention because it can foster self-reliance, deceive people about their need, and consume their hearts; yet the message broadens the warning to everyone. Rich or poor, no one can humble themselves, repent, and follow Jesus by natural ability alone.

The sermon’s answer is not despair but dependence on God. Jesus’ words, “with people it is impossible, but not with God,” direct listeners away from confidence in possessions, personal goodness, timing, or their own power to believe. Christians are urged to examine whether money owns their attention and trust, while unbelievers and false converts are called to abandon excuses, recognise their spiritual helplessness, and plead for God’s mercy. The application is wholehearted surrender: treasure Christ above wealth, relinquish pride and self-rule, and depend entirely on God to grant the faith and repentance needed to follow Jesus.

sermons.title: Praying For Spiritual Growth
sermons.summary:
What do we ask God to do in the lives of the people we love? Paul’s prayer in Philippians 1:9–11 directs our attention beyond comfortable circumstances to spiritual growth that brings glory to God. Even a church already active in gospel partnership needs to keep growing in love.

Biblical love is more than an emotion or a private feeling towards Jesus. It comes from God, takes its direction from Scripture and becomes visible in sacrificial service. Christ’s example challenges us to seek another person’s good instead of approaching church primarily as consumers. Growing knowledge should deepen obedience and sharpen our discernment about what is truly worthwhile.

Paul also prays for sincerity, blamelessness and righteous fruit. We are invited to examine our motives and conduct under the light of God’s Word, exposing hidden faults instead of covering them with a religious appearance. Spiritual maturity means pursuing holiness and refusing to remain content with yesterday’s growth.

These changes do not earn salvation. Righteous fruit depends on belonging to Christ, just as branches depend on the vine. The ultimate aim is God’s praise, not our own reputation. As we await Christ’s return, this prayer teaches us to seek increasing love, honest repentance and practical faithfulness for ourselves and our church.

sermons.title: Sacrificial Worship And Church Life Are Inseparable Part 2|  Romans 12:3-6
sermons.summary:
Offering a life to Christ takes practical shape in serving his people. Gratitude for God’s mercy should move believers beyond enjoying Christian teaching and worship towards costly care for the church. Receiving ministry from others and ministering to them belong together: devotion to Christ cannot be separated from concern for the body he loves.

Using Paul’s picture of a human body, the message explains how to think soberly about spiritual gifts. Each gift is received by grace, fitted to a particular contribution and intended for the common good. No member is unnecessary, and no gift provides grounds for pride or envy. Training can develop an ability God has given, but a qualification does not manufacture spiritual giftedness. Nor does possessing a prominent gift prove exceptional holiness. Faithfulness is shown in using what has been received, including quiet service that attracts little recognition.

Discovering a gift begins with dedication, love and involvement rather than waiting for a precise label. Believers are urged to offer their talents and skills, get to know fellow members and humbly ask where their service genuinely helps. Spiritual growth is not detached from these ordinary acts. Serving is both an expression of gratitude and an opportunity to draw nearer to Christ, trusting him to supply what is lacking.

sermons.title: The Work of Sanctification
sermons.summary:
Philippians 2:12–13 holds together the believer’s responsibility and God’s enabling work in sanctification. Paul points back to Christ’s humble obedience and tells his church to continue obeying, not only when a leader is present but even more in his absence. Working out salvation does not mean earning it. It means bringing the salvation received into practice through unity, humility, service and growing holiness.

This work requires effort, discipline and perseverance. Believers must hear God’s word in a way that leads to obedience, examine failures, resist laziness and pursue maturity with reverent fear and trembling. Leaders can teach and encourage, but each Christian remains responsible for responding and moving forward within the life of the church.

At the same time, no one sanctifies themselves by unaided strength. God is at work within his people, producing both the desire and the ability to do what pleases him. His power does not make human effort unnecessary; it makes faithful effort possible. This promise encourages believers when sin, weakness or hardship makes growth feel overwhelming. They are urged to run to Christ and to the church family God uses to help them. Rather than waiting passively, they can offer their lives in service, renew their minds and work diligently, trusting that God himself supplies the energy for every step of obedience.

sermons.title: The Glory of the God Man
sermons.summary:
John 1 announces the wonder that the eternal Word became flesh and lived among us. The sermon explains why Jesus must be both truly God and truly man: his divine nature gives his saving work infinite worth, his humanity makes him a fitting substitute for people, and his experience of temptation enables him to sympathise with human weakness without ever yielding to sin. The incarnation did not mean that the Son ceased to be God. Jesus remains one person with a divine nature and a sinless human nature, and he will remain the God-man for eternity.

From this foundation, the passage presents three great activities of Jesus. He displays God’s glory, not merely as visible brightness, but by revealing God’s truth, love, compassion, mercy, and character. Believers behold that glory in Scripture and are transformed as they receive more of Christ through God’s ordinary means of grace. Jesus also dispenses grace from his inexhaustible fullness: grace that pardons sinners and grace that empowers their growth. Finally, he defines and explains God, making the unseen Father known. Whether life presently feels successful, sorrowful, stressful, or stagnant, the sermon calls listeners to keep seeking Jesus in the Word, worship, prayer, baptism, and the Lord’s Table, receiving from the One who is their Prophet, Priest, and King.

sermons.title: Jesus Overcame the Devil's Temptations
sermons.summary:
Luke 4:1–13 recounts Jesus’ temptation in the wilderness. The preacher says the passage is first an invitation to behold Jesus as the faithful Son and representative, rather than merely a set of tactics for resisting temptation. After forty days without food, Jesus faces the devil’s offers at a point of real human weakness. Where Adam and Israel failed, the sermon presents Jesus as unwavering in his trust, worship and obedience. His responses from Scripture reveal the heart of each temptation, not just a convenient quotation to defeat an argument.

The first offer, turning stone to bread, is interpreted as a challenge to trust the Father’s care amid hunger. The offer of worldly kingdoms without the path of suffering presses Jesus to value a shortcut above worship of God alone. At the temple, a promise of angelic protection is used out of context to urge reckless self-direction. Jesus refuses to make God serve his own plans. The preacher invites listeners to admire the one who endured these pressures without yielding, and to find encouragement rather than despair when they recognise their own failures. Drawing on Hebrews, he urges those who struggle to approach Christ for mercy and help, trusting that this sympathetic high priest understands temptation and supplies grace in need.

sermons.title: Paul, the Exemplary Servant
sermons.summary:
Paul describes his life as a drink offering poured over the Philippians’ sacrifice and service of faith. The picture is one of willing devotion: his life belongs to Christ and is spent for Christ’s people. Imprisonment, hardship and the prospect of death do not make him resentful. Christ has changed him from a man concerned with status and achievement into a servant whose concern is the gospel and the church.

Such service remains genuinely joyful. Paul does not ask the Philippians to pity him; he rejoices that he can be spent for their faith and invites them to share that joy. His circumstances remain painful, but his satisfaction rests in Christ and in seeing believers live for Christ. Sacrifice and service belong together, and when they flow from union with Jesus they produce a joy the world cannot explain.

Paul’s example challenges a culture of receiving without giving. Christians are called to offer themselves as living sacrifices, help the weak and put other believers before personal comfort. They should consider what spiritual legacy their lives are forming: whom they encourage, where they pour out time and energy, and whether others can imitate their devotion. Such service may be costly, but it is not wasted. It honours God, strengthens his church and looks toward the eternal glory that outweighs present affliction.

sermons.title: The Resumé of a Humble Servant
sermons.summary:
Epaphroditus shows what humble Christian service looks like when it happens away from prominence. The Philippian church entrusted him with a long and difficult journey to support Paul in prison. Although little else is known about him, Paul describes him with remarkable warmth: a brother, fellow worker, fellow soldier, messenger and minister. His value did not come from a public position but from using his gifts faithfully for Christ and his people.

Each description reveals part of his character. As a brother, he shared genuine affection and family fellowship. As a worker, he served alongside Paul rather than watching from a distance. As a soldier, he accepted hardship and danger for the gospel. As the church’s messenger and minister, he completed their service to Paul at great personal cost, becoming sick and nearly dying in the work.

His compassion was equally striking. Even while ill, Epaphroditus was distressed because the Philippians were worried about him. Paul, though needing his help, sent him home so that they could rejoice. Their mutual concern models service that seeks another person’s good rather than personal comfort. Believers are urged to fight the good fight together, practise sincere love, meet needs, persevere in hardship and honour servants like him. Every gift can serve Christ, including faithful work that few people notice.

sermons.title: David's Example of Genuine Repentance
sermons.summary:
Psalm 51 records David’s prayer after Nathan confronted him about adultery and murder. The sermon uses his response to describe genuine repentance as reliance, eradication, and motivation. Repentance begins with reliance on God’s grace, not an attempt to become respectable before approaching him. David does not minimise his guilt or appeal to his achievements. He asks for mercy according to God’s loving kindness and compassion, and the message directs Christians to depend entirely on the cleansing secured through Jesus Christ.

Grace does not excuse continued sin. David asks God to blot out his transgressions, wash him thoroughly, and cleanse him. These images address the record of guilt, the inward defilement sin produces, and the need to be restored to communion with God. His motivation is an honest acknowledgment of the enormity of his sin, the God against whom he has sinned, and the corrupt desires from which sinful actions arise. He refuses blame-shifting and asks for truth in the innermost being. Listeners are urged to move beyond shallow confession of visible behaviour and ask God to expose the pride, control, selfishness, or other ruling desires beneath it. Genuine repentance runs toward grace, seeks the complete removal of sin, and longs above all for renewed fellowship with God.

sermons.title: In Christ Alone
sermons.summary:
Colossians 1:14 gives believers three reasons for lasting gratitude: union with Christ, redemption through Christ, and forgiveness because of Christ. Against the pressure of trials and discouragement, the message invites listeners to dwell on these spiritual blessings. Its central application is to cultivate thankfulness by remembering what God has already given, rather than allowing present difficulties to define the whole of life.

The words 'in whom' introduce the believer's intimate relationship with Jesus. Images of a building and foundation, branches and vine, body and head, and bride and bridegroom illustrate dependence, care and security. The preacher traces this union through salvation and explains redemption as release from slavery at a costly ransom. Christ's blood, not material wealth, provides the price, bringing freedom from sin's mastery and its penalty.

Forgiveness is presented as embracing all the believer's sins, with the removal of condemnation supplying grounds for assurance and joy. This confidence is not an invitation to continue pursuing sin: listeners are encouraged to resist temptation and find their satisfaction in Christ. Believers are urged to meditate on these gifts, speak about them with one another, and respond with gratitude through suffering. Those who have not trusted Christ are invited to turn from sin and come to him in faith.

sermons.title: An Example of the Gospel Truth
sermons.summary:
Life is brief, fragile, and moving toward eternity. Using passengers on a train, the sermon contrasts people consumed by status, safety, possessions, comfort, or entertainment with the wise person who looks beyond this life. Earthly achievements and belongings will soon lose their value, so believers should make present decisions in light of heaven and make their lives count for eternity.

Epaphras provides the example in Colossians 1. He spoke of Christ by teaching the gospel among people who did not know Him. Christians likewise remain on earth as Christ’s ambassadors, able to tell sinners about mercy while opportunity remains. Yet evangelism alone does not prove godliness. Epaphras was first a slave of Christ and then a faithful servant. His work flowed from belonging wholly to his Master rather than seeking importance or doing God a favour.

Recognising Christ’s ownership changes service into worship. Those who know their weakness depend on their Master for strength, provision, protection, joy, and love; His sufficiency is displayed through their work. Believers are called to speak of Christ, gladly submit their goals to Him, and serve faithfully and sacrificially. Unbelieving listeners are urged not to harden themselves against the gospel, but to come to Christ for forgiveness and new life under a gracious Master.

sermons.title: God's Goodness in a Sin Cursed World
sermons.summary:
Genesis 3:20–24 shows God’s goodness within a world damaged by human rebellion. Suffering, decay, and death did not arise from a defect in God’s creation but from sin and its consequences. Yet God continued to deal graciously with Adam and Eve. Adam’s naming of Eve as the mother of all living expresses faith in God’s promise that the woman’s offspring would defeat the serpent and reverse the curse. That faith, grounded in God’s word, gave him hope before the promised child appeared.

God’s provision of garments from animal skins supplied physical protection and pointed to the costly covering of guilt. The sacrificed animal anticipated the greater provision of Jesus Christ, whose death pays for his people’s sins and whose righteousness makes them acceptable to God. The sermon therefore calls believers to take sin seriously, confess it, and keep returning to Christ rather than hiding guilt through excuses or their own efforts. Finally, exclusion from the garden prevented humanity from living forever in a corrupted state. Though banishment revealed God’s holiness and the serious consequences of sin, it also preserved hope for redemption, resurrection, and a renewed creation. Christians can therefore face present suffering with gratitude, trusting God’s promises and looking to Christ’s return, when sin and its effects will be removed.

sermons.title: The Loving Redeemer
sermons.summary:
Colossians 1:18 presents Jesus Christ as the head of the body, the church, and calls believers to recognise his first place in everything. The sermon unfolds this picture through five aspects of Christ’s headship. He loves the church as his bride, shares with his people the blessings that belong to him, gives the church life, sustains its growth, and rules it as Lord. His people belong to him, yet he also gives himself to them with comfort, mercy, and strength. As every part of a body depends upon its head, the church receives life and direction from Christ. His resurrection as the firstborn from the dead confirms him as the living and reigning head who will never die again.

Christ supplies his church through the service of its members. Believers are therefore called to receive from him and use their gifts to build one another up in love, rather than blaming him for spiritual weakness while remaining inactive. Every ministry and gathering should be governed by Jesus and directed toward his honour. The sermon asks each listener to examine whether Christ has first place in relationships, work, worship, decisions, and desires. Because he is the loving Redeemer and supreme Lord, Christians can follow him willingly, treasure him above passing pleasures, and yield every area of life to his rule.

sermons.title: The Certainty of Christ and The Gospel
sermons.summary:
Opening a series through Luke’s Gospel, this sermon introduces both Luke’s distinctive portrait of Jesus and the certainty on which Christian faith rests. Matthew presents the promised King, Mark emphasizes the obedient servant, and John declares the Son of God; Luke especially portrays the Son of Man whose compassion reaches sinners, outsiders, sufferers, and the lost. Scenes unique to Luke reveal that compassion, including the father welcoming the prodigal son, Jesus praying for his executioners, and his care for people in distress. Yet the message asks an essential question: how can readers know these events are more than religious stories?

Luke’s prologue answers through the source, means, and purpose of his account. Its source is the testimony of many firsthand witnesses who saw Jesus’ works, heard his teaching, and served the message they received. Its means is Luke’s careful investigation of everything from the beginning and his deliberate arrangement of the material. Its purpose is that readers may know the certainty of what they have been taught. The sermon therefore rejects faith as a blind leap and presents Luke as a researched, trustworthy account of Jesus’ life, death, and resurrection. That certainty is intended to reshape life: listeners are called to anchor themselves in Christ, follow him despite opposition, cherish his compassion, and boldly share the truth about him.

sermons.title: Our Glorious Christ
sermons.summary:
The healing of blind Bartimaeus in Mark 10 presents Jesus as a servant King, a compassionate King, and an attractive King. Bartimaeus has nothing to offer and is ignored by the crowd, yet he recognises Jesus as the promised Son of David and cries for mercy. Unlike the rich ruler, who depends on his resources and walks away grieving, Bartimaeus approaches with empty hands, receives sight, and joyfully follows Jesus on the road. His greatest treasure is not restored eyesight but Christ Himself.

Jesus asks, “What do you want Me to do for you?” The question reveals the King who came to serve. Even as He travels toward the cross, Jesus stops for an overlooked beggar, identifies with his pain, and completely heals him. His compassion is neither distant pity nor reluctant assistance; it moves Him to meet weakness with mercy. Bartimaeus responds by calling Jesus Master, leaving his cloak, and following continually while glorifying God. The sermon invites needy people to ask this willing Saviour for salvation and urges believers first to receive Christ’s service before trying to serve Him. Having been served by Jesus, they can imitate His compassion and service. Christians are also challenged to identify whatever comforts or possessions hinder wholehearted discipleship and to follow their glorious King with gratitude and joy.

sermons.title: A Call To Self Examine
sermons.summary:
Self-examination can be uncomfortable, yet it exposes the pride and misplaced confidence that keep us from depending on Christ. At the Passover meal, Jesus confronts disciples who have argued about greatness and then announces that one of them will betray him. Their grief becomes a searching question about their own hearts, not simply an investigation of someone else.

The disciples’ reluctance to serve contrasts with Jesus washing their feet. Genuine humility takes practical shape in welcoming others, offering hospitality, praying for people and accepting the inconvenience of caring for them. Following Christ calls for sacrificial love rather than expecting the church to meet our preferences while we remain spectators.

Judas also warns against confusing an outwardly trustworthy reputation with genuine devotion. Money ruled his heart, while the other disciples did not recognise his betrayal. We are urged to examine whether possessions, family, comfort or security have become more important to us than Jesus. God’s sovereign purpose does not excuse Judas’s responsibility for rejecting him.

The warning leads to an invitation, not hopelessness. Jesus willingly gave himself as the perfect sacrifice for sinners. Honest examination should move us away from self-trust and towards repentance, faith in Christ and a growing willingness to love and serve his people.

sermons.title: A Joyful Healthy Church
sermons.summary:
Paul’s greeting in Philippians shows that a joyful, healthy church begins with Christ rather than favourable circumstances. Although Paul writes from prison, he calls believers to rejoice in the Lord. His own life demonstrates that Christian joy can endure suffering because it rests in Christ, the gospel, and God’s continuing grace. By calling himself and Timothy bond-servants, Paul models humble devotion to the Master who bought His people out of slavery to sin.

That devotion is lived out together. Believers are saints set apart for Christ and joined to His people, not isolated individuals. They are called to use their gifts, serve one another, make disciples, and receive the care and teaching of faithful church leaders. Paul’s words, “grace to you and peace,” also remind Christians that God supplies the grace needed for growth, obedience, service, and calm assurance amid trouble. The sermon therefore asks each member to consider whether they are living as Christ’s servant within His body. A church grows in health and joy as its people rest in Christ, depend on His grace, love His household, build up fellow believers, and follow leaders who faithfully teach God’s Word.

sermons.title: Christ is Everything!
sermons.summary:
At the close of Colossians, the sermon gathers the book’s message around one conviction: Christ is everything. Paul has presented Jesus as supreme in creation and the church, sufficient for salvation, and worthy to shape every part of a believer’s life. The closing greetings are therefore more than polite farewells. They reveal Christ-centred fellowship as churches and households welcome one another, Christ-centred proclamation as Paul’s letter is read aloud, and Christ-centred calling as Archippus is urged to fulfil the ministry he received in the Lord.

Nympha’s open home illustrates how ordinary resources can be devoted to serving Christ, while the exchange of letters shows why the word must be proclaimed even when it confronts false teaching or personal pride. Every believer has a distinct calling, but each calling comes from the same Lord and is carried out for his honour rather than personal recognition. The sermon challenges listeners not to let their gifts rust through neglect or to hide behind uncertainty about how they can serve. Instead, they are invited to consider what God has entrusted to them, take their responsibility seriously, and join other faithful servants in fellowship, proclamation, and ministry—even when service involves sacrifice.

sermons.title: What True Repentance is Not
sermons.summary:
Preaching from Luke 3:7–11, the speaker asks what genuine repentance looks like as John the Baptist prepares people for Jesus. He warns against treating baptism or other religious activities as a way to earn salvation. Nor can a family connection, even descent from Abraham or a godly home, transfer faith to another person. John's image of an axe already at the roots gives the appeal urgency: do not postpone turning from self-reliance to Christ. The preacher insists that Jesus alone is the refuge for sinners, while the fruit of repentance is evidence of new life rather than its purchase price.

The sermon then considers John's practical answer to people asking what they should do. Sharing an extra garment and food with someone in need illustrates fruit visible in ordinary life. The preacher is careful not to present generosity as another ladder to acceptance with God. Instead, he describes a person resting in Christ, whose kindness awakens a desire to reflect Christ's care for others. He challenges both those relying on religious performance and those delaying repentance to come to Jesus now. Believers are encouraged to trust him beyond the beginning of salvation and to show compassion, especially within the household of faith, in deed as well as words.

sermons.title: How To Apply the Knowledge of God's Will
sermons.summary:
Colossians 1:9–11 shows that knowing God’s will is meant to transform the whole Christian life. Paul does not pray for knowledge that remains in the mind or produces only impressive discussion. Believers are to be filled with God’s truth so that they walk in a manner worthy of Jesus Christ. This walk follows Jesus, obeys him as Lord when others turn away, and gives devotion to him alone.

The purpose of this walk is to please God in every area of life. Christians do not earn acceptance through good works; they seek to please the Father because Christ has already brought them forgiveness and adoption. Paul identifies two inseparable features of this growth. Believers bear fruit in every good work, persevering through hard circumstances and difficult people with steadfast, joyful patience. They also increase in a personal, intimate knowledge of God, not merely information about him. As they find their deepest delight in his presence, they receive strength to endure and serve without resentment. The sermon calls listeners to study God’s Word deeply, follow Christ with complete obedience, work actively for his kingdom, and seek fellowship with God as their greatest satisfaction. When knowledge leads to loving communion and fruitful action, the Father is honoured and the believer’s life fulfils its intended purpose.

sermons.title: Our God Provides
sermons.summary:
From Philippians 4:19–20, this sermon celebrates God as the provider of his people. Paul has received the Philippians’ generous support and assures them that God will supply every need according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus. This is not a blank promise that every desire will be fulfilled or that believers will always become wealthy. It is confidence that the personal, faithful Father knows what his children require to continue faithfully in the life and service he gives them. God’s provision includes ordinary gifts as well as spiritual blessings, and it flows from his abundant riches rather than reluctant leftovers.

The promise is especially connected to a church that has sacrificed for gospel ministry. The Philippians gave from poverty, and Paul trusts God to care for them more generously than they could care for him. Jesus is the channel through whom believers receive forgiveness, adoption, the Holy Spirit, peace, wisdom, strength, inheritance, and daily necessities. The proper response is worship: giving God glory, thanking him for his gifts, working diligently with the means he provides, and using resources for his kingdom rather than self-indulgence. The sermon urges believers to distinguish needs from wants, seek God’s kingdom first, refuse anxiety about tomorrow, and answer his faithful provision with confident, wholehearted praise.

sermons.title: The Greatest Person
sermons.summary:
Mark 10:45 gathers the message of Mark’s Gospel into one sentence: the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve and give His life as a ransom for many. Jesus corrects His disciples’ pursuit of status by redefining greatness. In His kingdom, greatness is not measured by comfort, possessions, influence, or the number of people who serve us. It is seen in sacrificial love, humble service, and labour for the good of others and the advance of the gospel.

The sermon traces six features of Jesus’ greatness. He is the supreme example and the glorious Son of Man with everlasting dominion, yet He denies Himself and takes the place of a servant. His service reaches its height in the cross, where He willingly gives His life as the ransom price that frees His people from slavery to sin. He acts as their substitute, taking what belongs to them and granting what belongs to Him. This good news calls unbelievers to repent and trust wholly in Christ rather than their own efforts. It also calls believers to love, fear, praise, and imitate their Saviour. Following Jesus means laying down personal rights, serving fellow believers, and accepting costly labour together for the spread of His name.

sermons.title: The Christ-Centered Wife
sermons.summary:
Explaining Colossians 3:18, this sermon places a wife’s submission within the larger vision of Christ’s supremacy. Marriage cannot be understood rightly when separated from Jesus, because he is the source of salvation, peace, strength, and satisfaction. The sermon presents marriage as God’s design and distinguishes equal personal value from different roles. Submission does not mean abandoning rational thought, agreeing with everything, placing a husband above Christ, or obeying direction contrary to God’s Word. Nor does the command permit a husband to coerce, manipulate, or demand submission. Rather, a wife is called to come willingly under her own husband’s leadership as an act of devotion to the Lord.

Drawing on Ephesians 5, the sermon describes marriage as a visible picture of Christ and the church. A wife’s deepest identity and well-being are therefore found in Christ rather than in the conduct of a fallen husband. From that security, she can express respect, offer thoughtful counsel, avoid persistent contention, and support her husband’s decisions even when she would have chosen differently. The message also calls husbands to reject entitlement and recognises the difficulty of following selfish or unreasonable leadership. Its central appeal is for wives to delight in Christ’s lordship and let their conduct display the church’s willing devotion to him, while keeping obedience to God as the governing boundary.

sermons.title: Jesus' Illegitimate Trial
sermons.summary:
Jesus stands before hostile religious leaders as the innocent Saviour who willingly suffers for sinners. Following Mark 14, the message traces his abandonment, the attempts to manufacture a case against him, and the violence that follows his declaration of who he is. The contrast is striking: those entrusted with judging others pursue a predetermined death sentence, while the accused remains truthful, obedient and free from retaliation.

The trial exposes the failure of the witnesses and the distortion of Jesus’ words about the temple. His silence under false accusation reveals patient strength rather than helplessness. When asked whether he is the Christ and the Son of God, he answers openly and warns that the one they are judging will himself exercise divine authority. His innocence matters because sinners need a substitute whose obedience, as well as his suffering, meets their need before God.

The closing challenge moves from the courtroom to the listener’s heart. Religious hostility is not a reason to feel morally superior, but a warning about pride and the need for grace. Christ’s willing love calls for trust, gratitude and a life devoted to him. That response includes relinquishing bitterness, humbling ourselves towards fellow believers and pursuing united service for the gospel.

sermons.title: From Mega Fear to Mega Joy
sermons.summary:
In Luke's account of the shepherds who hear of Jesus' birth, the preacher traces a movement from fear to joy and from hearing to action. The shepherds are portrayed as people of low standing, startled by the angel and God's glory. The angel's announcement is good news for them: a Saviour, Christ the Lord, has been born. The preacher dwells on those titles to explain why the child is the source of joy, and on the manger to show the humility of one who comes near to the lowly. He urges listeners to know themselves truthfully before God and receive Christ joyfully rather than trusting their own importance.

The sermon then follows the shepherds' response. They hear the heavenly praise, go promptly to see the child, tell others what they were told, and return glorifying God. The preacher distinguishes mere amazement from Mary's treasuring and pondering of these events, inviting a response that reaches the heart and changes priorities. He calls believers to praise Christ, seek him eagerly and proclaim him without shame. Reluctance to share the good news, he suggests, may call for renewed humility and deeper delight in the Saviour rather than simply more confidence in one's own ability.

sermons.title: The Transcendence and Immanence of God | Sunday Teachings
sermons.summary:
God is exalted above everything he has made, yet he is not distant from the lives of his people.
