Listeners are encouraged to put love into deeds within their local fellowship and to speak the gospel boldly, trusting God rather than themselves to give life through his word.

sermons.title: The Growing Christian - Part 2
sermons.summary:
Philippians 3:15–16 describes the attitude of a growing Christian. Paul admits that he has not reached holiness, yet he refuses to stand still. He presses toward Christ and calls mature believers to share that mindset. Maturity is not sinlessness or merely knowing correct doctrine. It is a continuing life of visible fruit, awareness of sin, love for Jesus, and progress through trials. Suffering can become an opportunity for growth when Christians trust God’s sovereignty, give thanks, and use hardship to advance the gospel rather than retreat into complaint.

This growth begins in the mind. Believers are to adopt the humble, self-giving attitude of Christ, count lesser gains as loss beside knowing him, and protect their thinking from worldly clutter and deception. Scripture, prayer, worship, service, and fellowship train the mind to look toward eternal things. When Christians hold a different attitude from God’s Word, Paul trusts God to reveal and correct it—sometimes through Scripture, other believers, or loving discipline. The mature should therefore remain patient with those who are growing. Finally, believers must keep walking by the standard they have received. The sermon calls listeners to stay on the path of Scripture, follow godly examples, fight sin, seek communion with Christ, value his people, and keep running toward him with their eyes fixed on the finish.

sermons.title: The Immutability Of God | Sunday Teachings
sermons.summary:
In a world of shifting circumstances and fragile commitments, God’s unchanging character gives his people a dependable place to rest. His immutability means that his being, purposes and promises do not deteriorate or need improvement. Unlike creatures who gain knowledge, lose strength and revise plans, God remains perfect and faithful in all that he is.

The message connects this truth with the security of his love and the reliability of his promises. His purposes are not revised because of unexpected events, and his gracious commitment is not exhausted by the weakness of those he saves. Such assurance is presented as a reason to pursue holiness, not permission to ignore sin. Believers are urged to hold closely to God’s promises instead of remembering them only occasionally while other concerns dominate their hearts.

Unchangeableness does not make God cold, inactive or unable to relate to his people. His continuing care and Christ’s faithful work show personal involvement rather than indifference. The closing application comforts struggling believers while warning against assuming that God will eventually overlook unbelief or abandon his judgement. The invitation is to come to Jesus with guilt and need, trusting his promise to receive those who come and relying on his grace for forgiveness, repentance and a changed heart.

sermons.title: Wars And Rumors Of Wars
sermons.summary:
Studying the end times is presented as a way to live more faithfully now, not merely gather information about the future. Focusing on Mark 13:7–8, the preacher considers Jesus' warning about wars and rumours of wars alongside his command not to be frightened. He interprets the conflicts as intensifying birth pains before Christ's return, and connects that reading with passages in Daniel and Revelation.

The message traces a progression of conflict involving nations, the Antichrist and opposition to God's people, culminating in Christ's decisive judgment. Through these scenes, the recurring emphasis is God's sovereignty. Events do not unfold beyond his knowledge or control, even though sinful people remain responsible for their actions. The ground of the believer's confidence is the character of the God who governs history and loves his people, rather than confidence that history will remain peaceful.

The conclusion returns to present priorities. If earthly security and possessions cannot last, they must not become the foundation of hope. Believers are urged to loosen their attachments to passing comforts, place their hope in Christ's coming and remain faithful through suffering. Those who do not know him are invited to seek forgiveness now. Salvation is offered through the merciful Saviour, not earned through works or a particular religious feeling.

sermons.title: One is Coming Who is Mightier
sermons.summary:
From Luke 3:14–16, the preacher contrasts John the Baptist with the far mightier Christ to whom John points. He first recalls John's answers to tax collectors and soldiers: genuine repentance should become visible in honesty, restraint and contentment rather than misuse of power. Yet neither these actions nor water baptism can cleanse the heart by themselves. When the crowds wonder whether John is the Messiah, John plainly refuses that place and directs their expectation beyond himself. The sermon asks listeners not to anchor their hope in even the most admired human leader.

The preacher then explores Christ's might and worth. John's statement that he is unworthy to untie the coming one's sandals becomes a call to humility and worship. John can baptize with water, but Jesus can baptize with the Holy Spirit; the preacher describes the Spirit's work in cleansing, strengthening and uniting believers. He also interprets baptism with fire as a warning of judgment, not an experience to seek. The sermon invites believers to return to Christ with renewed joy instead of being distracted by lesser things. Those who do not know him are urged to trust him rather than their background or works, and not to dismiss the seriousness of rejecting him.

sermons.title: The Christ-Centered Child
sermons.summary:
Explaining Colossians 3:20, this sermon addresses children who still depend on their parents for care, training, and discipline. God has designed every family role to display Christ, and children do this by obeying their parents. Obedience means listening attentively under their authority, receiving instruction, accepting correction, and following directions even when a command is unwelcome or not fully understood. It also includes inward honour: children are not merely to perform an outward task while belittling, arguing with, mocking, or resenting the parents God has placed over them. The governing exception is any command contrary to God’s will, because God remains the highest authority.

The motive reaches beyond avoiding discipline or gaining a reward. Obedience pleases the Lord and expresses trust that God wisely gave children parents who seek their good. Since young people lack experience and struggle with selfish desires, parental guidance provides loving eyes outside themselves. The sermon connects this calling to Jesus, who honoured and obeyed his Father completely, even through suffering. Children are urged to respond immediately rather than delay, complete the whole task rather than stop partway, and obey willingly rather than with complaining body language. Both children and parents are directed to Christ for forgiveness, changed hearts, and strength to make family obedience an act of worship.

sermons.title: Use Your Spiritual Gifts Part 2
sermons.summary:
Spiritual gifts are discovered through loving service, not by making self-discovery the centre of Christian life. The call is to pursue Christ by caring for his church. As believers give themselves to the needs around them, particular abilities become useful and recognisable. Knowing a gift then brings responsibility to use it, rather than remaining a consumer of teaching or waiting for a formal position.

Paul’s instructions connect each gift with the character needed to exercise it well. Encouragement brings God’s promises to people facing weariness, temptation or suffering. Giving should be sincere and generous, free from the desire for recognition or repayment. Leadership means caring for others with diligence, enthusiasm and commitment, not controlling them or serving reluctantly. Mercy notices hidden pain and offers compassionate help with cheerfulness, without adding the burden of a helper’s resentment. These gifts support the church’s unity and growth together with preaching, teaching and practical service.

The application is personal and practical: learn promises that can strengthen a struggling believer, share generously, take responsibility eagerly and approach hurting people with genuine warmth. Love for Jesus cannot remain detached from love for his body. Whatever gifts God has given, they are to be offered gratefully for his glory and the good of fellow believers.

sermons.title: The Mystery of Christ in Us
sermons.summary:
Colossians 1:26–27 unveils a mystery hidden through past ages but now made known to all God’s people: Christ in you, the hope of glory. This mystery is not a puzzle discovered by intelligence or reserved for an elite. God chose to reveal it by grace to saints, including Gentile believers outside Israel’s privileges. The astonishing truth is not merely that Christ gives blessings, stands beside his people, or thinks about them. The glorious Christ himself makes his home in them. The Creator dwells within his creatures, the sinless one within people struggling with sin, making this revelation humbling and wonderful.

The mystery is rich because the all-sufficient Christ is not distant. Believers possess him securely, may enjoy his presence, and are themselves possessed and ruled by him. He comforts, cleanses, strengthens, reshapes priorities, and creates a desire to obey from the heart. His indwelling power enables holiness and endurance through trials. Christ in his people is also their hope of glory—a confident expectation that he will carry them into resurrection life, fellowship, and the new creation. The sermon calls Christians to stop envying worldly advantages and instead seek a deeper experience of belonging to Jesus. Those outside Christ are invited to call on him for mercy, forgiveness, and the new life of his presence within.

sermons.title: Do Not Lie to One Another
sermons.summary:
Working through Colossians 3:9–11, this sermon calls Christians to refuse every form of intentional deception within the church. Lying includes exaggeration, false impressions, flattering words, misleading expressions, and pretending that personal or family life is stronger than it really is. Honest speech can feel vulnerable, especially when a congregation has become condemning or ungracious. Believers should therefore examine whether their manner makes weaker brothers and sisters feel unsafe. Yet another person’s harshness never excuses dishonesty; Christians are commanded to speak truth even when openness is costly.

Paul supplies three motivations for this truthful life. First, the old self devoted to self-protection has been laid aside, while a new self loyal to Christ has been received. Second, that new self is being renewed in true knowledge toward the image of its Creator. Seeking likeness to Jesus, who embodies truth, cannot be reconciled with deceiving one another. Third, Christ has broken down religious, cultural, ethnic, and social barriers to form one united people. Because trust sustains relationships, lies attack the unity Christ purchased. The sermon urges believers to remember their new Master, reject image management, and practise sincere, gracious honesty that honours Christ and strengthens his church.

sermons.title: Effective Evangelism - Part 1
sermons.summary:
Colossians 4:2–4 presents effective evangelism as a work sustained by dependence on God rather than personal confidence. Paul’s instruction to devote ourselves to prayer calls believers to pray persistently, alertly, and with thanksgiving. Thanksgiving matters because it fixes the heart on God’s power, love, sovereignty, and patience, even when opportunities are missed, witness is rejected, or faithfulness brings suffering. Prayer therefore does more than request open doors; it shapes the evangelist for endurance, compassion, and trust.

Paul also asks the church to pray that God would open a door for the word and help him declare the mystery of Christ clearly. His imprisonment shows the sacrificial spirit of gospel ministry: he values opportunities to speak about Christ more than comfort or release. The sermon urges believers to surrender pride, status, and convenience, and to see hardship as an opportunity for faithful witness. It also warns against three barriers to clarity—speaking from emotion without thought, overwhelming listeners with excessive information, and using unexplained Christian terminology. Effective witness communicates the holiness of God, human sin, and Christ as the saving substitute in language people can understand. Believers are therefore encouraged to sharpen their understanding, explain repentance and faith plainly, and seek the listener’s genuine comprehension rather than merely completing a religious duty.

sermons.title: God Is Sovereign Over Our Salvation | Mark 12:10-11 Part 2
sermons.summary:
Salvation is not a fragile human achievement that God merely assists. Mark 12:11 directs attention to the Lord's work and the wonder it should awaken. Reading Jesus' words alongside Psalm 118, the sermon connects the rejected stone becoming the cornerstone with God becoming his people's salvation. It develops that theme through election, redemption and protection.

Election is presented as God's gracious choice rather than a response to superior goodness, potential or independently produced faith. Redemption likewise rests on Christ: he bears sin's judgement and grants righteousness to people unable to rescue themselves. The message then applies the same divine sovereignty to preservation. The God who begins this saving work keeps his people, giving them grounds for assurance beyond their own performance. Christ's care and the Father's power are presented as reasons to trust rather than live in continual fear of being lost.

These convictions are intended to produce humility, gratitude and active devotion, not passivity. Believers have no basis for boasting, because salvation displays God's undeserved love. They are urged to dedicate their lives to him and continue sharing the gospel even when others resist. The outcome does not rest on the messenger's strength. Confidence in God's saving power makes participation in his work a privilege rather than an anxious burden.

sermons.title: A Call to Rejoice
sermons.summary:
Philippians 4:4–5 commands believers to rejoice in the Lord always and to let their gentle spirit be known to everyone. This joy is not a passing mood produced by comfortable circumstances, possessions, relationships or successful ministry. Paul writes while confined and opposed, yet repeats the command because Christian joy is rooted in the unchanging person of Jesus Christ. The sermon describes joy as deep satisfaction in what the heart loves and urges believers to examine whether disappointment reveals that they have placed their hope in something other than the Lord.

Christians can rejoice through trials because Christ is near, salvation is secure, and the Holy Spirit’s joy is already present in them. They cultivate that joy by remembering God’s saving work, looking to Christ, praying, reading Scripture, worshipping, serving and trusting God’s providence. Rejoicing does not deny pain; it views every circumstance under God’s wise care and remembers that Christ will return. Joy then becomes visible as gentleness, patience, graciousness and peace toward both believers and unbelievers. The message calls the church to reject grumbling and harshness, encourage one another with joyful faith, and present the good news of Christ with a manner that matches its hope.

sermons.title: More than Awe, Finish Strong
sermons.summary:
Continuing Luke's account of Jesus' presentation at the temple, the preacher considers Mary and Joseph's amazement at Simeon's words. He says the child's identity and mission are still unfolding before them: Jesus is God's salvation, and Simeon's earlier prayer reaches beyond Israel to the Gentiles. Yet amazement alone is only a beginning. Simeon's further words announce that the child will be opposed and will bring both falling and rising. The preacher understands this as a division made visible in people's response to Jesus. Even Mary will suffer deeply as opposition to her son reaches its terrible height, and that opposition exposes what is in human hearts.

The sermon then turns to Anna, whose long devotion is expressed in prayer, fasting, thanksgiving and telling others about the child. Her faithfulness offers a contrast to mere wonder or resistance. The preacher asks listeners not simply to be impressed by Christ, but to receive him and remain devoted to him. He challenges the idea that service can wait until a comfortable retirement or must stop with old age. Anna's example encourages both younger and older believers to serve with what they can do, including prayer and witness, and to finish their lives faithfully rather than drift into self-centred ease.

sermons.title: The Love Within the Gospel Truth
sermons.summary:
Paul’s gratitude for the Colossians includes their “love in the Spirit,” love directed toward the saints in their local church. This is not an optional addition to holiness or service. It is the greatest Christian virtue, the bond of unity, and the foundation that gives substance to every gift used for believers’ good. When Christians serve without love, even outwardly impressive activity becomes hollow.

The sermon traces this love to three causes. First, the Holy Spirit gives new birth, making believers children of one Father and drawing them toward others who share the same Christ and indwelling Spirit. Second, the gospel displays Christ’s willing, costly love for the people He redeemed. Those who treasure Him are compelled to honour and care for those whom He loves. Third, hope laid up in heaven loosens the grip of self-love, comfort, possessions, and self-preservation. Looking to Christ enables believers to invest now in the people with whom they will share eternity.

Such love also strengthens the church’s witness. When people of different backgrounds gladly open their homes, sacrifice time and resources, and draw nearer in fellowship, unbelievers see something that self-interest cannot explain. The sermon therefore urges Christians to yield to the Spirit, meditate on the gospel and future hope, and actively meet the needs of their brothers and sisters.

sermons.title: The Benefits and the Blessings of The Lord
sermons.summary:
Psalm 103 calls a weary soul to pause, rise above daily distraction, and remember the goodness of God. David is not describing an enemy or presenting a complaint; he is speaking to his own soul and summoning every part of himself to bless the Lord. The sermon explains that blessing God means proclaiming his goodness with genuine inward worship rather than offering words while the heart remains occupied elsewhere. Spiritual apathy grows when God’s benefits slip from memory, leaving gratitude to be displaced by pride, control, selfishness, or the pursuit of approval.

David therefore tells his soul to forget none of God’s benefits. The message follows five gifts: God pardons every iniquity, heals the soul’s diseases, redeems life from the pit, crowns his people with loving kindness and compassion, and satisfies them with good things. These benefits are presented as the fruit of Christ’s saving work, not rewards for personal merit. Remembering them is described as preaching the gospel to one’s own soul. Listeners are urged to slow down, deliberately recall God’s mercy, and seek lasting satisfaction in fellowship with Christ rather than in temporary comforts. As gratitude grows, God renews the inner person and carries believers above their trials, moving them to praise him sincerely and let his goodness shape their relationships and conduct.

sermons.title: A Plea To The Unconverted | Mark: 14:21
sermons.summary:
Jesus’ warning about his betrayer in Mark 14:21 brings together the certainty of God’s purpose and the seriousness of human responsibility. The message first considers the Son of Man as the divine and human Saviour whose obedience and sacrifice provide refuge for sinners. His journey to the cross fulfils God’s revealed plan, rather than representing a defeat that catches God by surprise.

That sovereignty does not excuse Judas’s betrayal. The preacher holds together God’s rule over events and the sinner’s accountability, while insisting that evil arises from the human heart and that God is not its author. Judas’s closeness to Jesus makes his rejection especially sobering. Hearing the gospel, understanding its message and witnessing its effects are distinguished from personally trusting Christ. Greater exposure to the invitation is presented as greater responsibility, not a substitute for faith.

The warning then turns towards the reality and permanence of judgment and the danger of delaying repentance. Its purpose is to urge honest self-examination and an immediate response to the Saviour’s offer of forgiveness. Neither deep guilt nor religious respectability should become a reason to stay away from him. Believers are also challenged to share the gospel faithfully, beginning with loved ones and children rather than treating the warning as someone else’s concern.

sermons.title: The Denial Of The Ages
sermons.summary:
Peter's repeated denial of Jesus is a warning that sincere devotion and past experience do not make a believer immune to serious failure. Set against the joy available in Christ, his bitter collapse invites honest examination of the attitudes that gradually weaken dependence on the Lord. The account in Mark 14 is approached not as an occasion to condemn Peter from a distance, but as a warning every Christian needs.

The sermon traces four connected steps: confidence in personal strength, spiritual apathy, self-directed decisions, and exposure to dangerous temptation. Peter dismisses Jesus' warning, sleeps instead of watching and praying, acts without submitting to his Master's purpose, and enters circumstances he cannot handle. His escalating denials reveal the consequences of a decline that began before anyone questioned him. Responsibility cannot simply be shifted onto the people or pressures around him.

The practical response is humble dependence rather than stronger claims of personal resolve. Believers are urged to acknowledge their vulnerability, seek Christ in prayer, obey his word instead of following comfort or feeling, and welcome godly counsel. Choosing fellowship that encourages faithfulness also means refusing compromises that feed temptation. The call is to take Christ's warnings seriously and pursue the joy of walking closely with him.

sermons.title: God's Goodness And The Vine-growers Corruption Mark 12:1-9
sermons.summary:
God's generous care is met with astonishing resistance in the parable of the vineyard. Mark 12:1–9 portrays an owner who provides everything needed for fruitfulness, only to have his messengers abused and his beloved son killed. The sermon reads this as Jesus' searching confrontation with religious leaders who claim authority while withholding the worship and obedience due to God.

The vineyard's provision displays God's goodness, and the request for fruit expresses his rightful claim. Yet the tenants treat stewardship as ownership. Their escalating violence reveals the danger of self-righteousness, greed and the desire to receive praise that belongs to God. Sending the beloved son brings the owner's patience into sharp focus; rejecting him also brings the certainty of judgement. Religious position cannot protect leaders who refuse the Son and misdirect the people entrusted to them.

Two responses shape the closing application: rejoice in Christ's victory and take God's word seriously. His death is not an unexpected defeat, but the means by which he bears his people's sin and brings them to God. Listeners are urged to examine whether Christ truly holds their allegiance, rather than trusting attendance, knowledge or appearances. The invitation is to receive his righteousness and live in grateful love, obedience and joy under his rightful care.

sermons.title: The Family Tree of Salvation
sermons.summary:
The preacher approaches Luke 3:23–38, the genealogy of Jesus, as more than a difficult list of names. He says the family line places Jesus in real human history and invites listeners to see why he is the Savior they need. He organizes the sermon around five relationships in the list. As the supposed son of Joseph, Jesus entered ordinary human life while, in the preacher's account, Joseph was his legal rather than biological father. He connects this with Jesus' sinless life and his ability to act for sinners. As David's son, Jesus is presented as the promised king; as Abraham's son, the one through whom blessing reaches the nations.

Tracing the line further to Adam, the preacher contrasts the disobedience associated with the first man with Christ's obedience and his bearing of sin's curse. He then distinguishes Jesus' sonship of God from being a child of God by creation or adoption, proclaiming him divine. These are theological conclusions the preacher draws from the genealogy and related passages, not an invitation to guess at unknown names. He urges listeners to bring suffering and guilt to Christ, trust him as king and blessing giver, and worship him as the Son of God. The sermon closes by asking for deeper satisfaction in knowing Jesus.

sermons.title: Are You Willing to Fully Embrace Christ?
sermons.summary:
From Luke 3:18–20, the preacher considers how John the Baptist's ministry embodied his witness to the mighty Christ. He presents three responses for those who embrace Jesus: proclaim him boldly, confront significant sin lovingly, and accept the cost of faithfulness. John's repeated preaching of the gospel is described as more than detached information. It included warning, pleading, urgency and comfort, as he called people to trust Christ rather than themselves. The preacher cautions against insisting that only one tone can communicate the gospel, while keeping the offer of Christ at the center.

John also rebuked Herod's public wrongdoing without favoritism. The preacher says such confrontation was not a claim that moral improvement saves; it exposed the need for Christ and protected people affected by corrupt leadership. Herod responded by imprisoning John. Listeners are urged not to harden themselves when corrected but to bring their sin to the Savior who can forgive and strengthen them. The preacher rejects the idea that John's shortened ministry was a failure measured by popularity or length. He argues that faithfulness is the better measure. Rather than copying John's exact calling, believers should speak of Christ and resist compromise wherever they have been placed, trusting him amid possible cost.

sermons.title: Let Us Now Praise Christ
sermons.summary:
Zechariah’s prophecy in Luke 1 is presented as a song of praise, not merely a lesson about how salvation works. The preacher invites listeners to behold Jesus as a compassionate savior, a loving redeemer and a mighty king. He also pauses over Zechariah being filled with the Holy Spirit: praise that honours Christ is the fitting response to God’s work, and believers are urged to yield to the Spirit’s guidance.

God’s visit to his people means decisive intervention, not a casual call. The preacher traces earlier acts of deliverance before describing Jesus coming personally into a world marked by sin and self-righteousness. Redemption is pictured as release from slavery through a costly purchase: Christ’s death frees his people from sin’s penalty and gives them freedom to resist its power. The “horn of salvation” then points to royal strength, seen in Christ’s victory and anticipated in his future reign.

This praise calls for more than distant admiration. Believers are encouraged to resist sin, delight in Christ and give him their daily lives. Those who do not know him are invited to come helplessly and rest in his saving power rather than trust their own works.

sermons.title: Let Us Praise The Lord
sermons.summary:
Mary’s praise in Luke 1:46–50 directs attention away from herself and toward Jesus Christ. Though she is a young, obscure servant, she rejoices in “God my Saviour” and magnifies the Lord who has looked on her lowly condition. Her blessing does not arise from personal holiness or social importance, but from the mighty Saviour dwelling within her. The sermon therefore invites every believer to join Mary, receive Christ with empty hands, and let inward joy become public praise rather than private, silent feeling.

Mary celebrates three divine perfections in the Saviour: his might, holiness, and mercy. His power accomplishes what is impossible, defeats sin and death, and can soften the hardest heart. His holiness means that he is beautiful beyond comparison and worthy of wholehearted worship. His mercy bends toward guilty, undeserving people, reaches through every generation, and is seen most clearly in Christ. The fear of God mentioned in Mary’s song is not a price that earns mercy; it is the awed response mercy creates in those who have received it. Listeners are called to turn from apathy and complacency, fix their attention on the mighty, holy, merciful Saviour, speak of him openly, and receive him by faith without presenting personal merit as a qualification.

sermons.title: Complete Devotion to God
sermons.summary:
Romans 12:1 calls every Christian to complete devotion to God. Paul’s appeal rests on the mercies unfolded throughout Romans: justification, peace, reconciliation, grace, adoption, hope, resurrection, and the inseparable love of God in Christ. Believers do not offer themselves in order to earn mercy. Because God has already shown mercy through Jesus, gratitude becomes the motive for a wholehearted response. Healthy doctrine fuels godly living, and a clear view of the gospel moves Christians to place their lives at God’s disposal.

Paul describes this response as presenting the body as a living and holy sacrifice. The body is not evil, but it carries desires that resist holiness and must be brought under the Spirit’s rule. To present it is a decisive commitment, like an enduring vow; to be holy is to belong entirely to God without reserving cherished sins, relationships, plans, or pleasures; and to be living is to continue that dedication through ordinary life. Christian worship therefore extends beyond gathered meetings into work, rest, conversation, relationships, thoughts, and choices. The sermon does not promise sinless perfection, but calls believers to fight sin and embrace God’s commands for life. Such surrender is pleasing worship, frees Christians from being ruled by fear or worldly ambition, and prepares them to remain faithful when obedience becomes costly.

sermons.title: I Love You, Oh Yahweh
sermons.summary:
Looking back over a lifetime of danger and deliverance, David begins Psalm 18 with an intensely personal declaration of love for God. The sermon urges believers to learn from that gratitude rather than allowing prayer to become only a list of requests. David remembers God as his rock, fortress, deliverer, shield, salvation, and stronghold. Each image presents God as a mighty warrior who protects those who take refuge in him, yet also as a personal saviour whom David can call “my God.”

The Psalm’s dramatic language pictures God hearing David’s distressed cry and moving with power to rescue him. The sermon connects these images to Christ, encouraging listeners to remember the ways God has sustained them through trials and to grow in thankful affection rather than treating his help as an obligation. David says that God brought him into a broad place because he delighted in him, and the message emphasises that rescue flows from loving commitment, not reluctance. Listeners who feel overwhelmed or ashamed are invited to call on God, remember his past faithfulness, and reject the idea that repeated need exhausts his compassion. The fitting response is confident prayer, grateful praise, and a heart that openly loves the one who has been a refuge through every battle.

sermons.title: Jesus Is The Passover
sermons.summary:
As betrayal and death approach, is Jesus at the mercy of those plotting against him? The preparations for the Passover in Mark 14:12–16 reveal a Saviour who remains in control. His authority is not diminished by his willingness to suffer; he gives his life according to God’s purpose.

The Passover points beyond deliverance from Egypt to the greater redemption accomplished by Christ. Its sacrificial lambs direct our attention to the sinless Saviour, whose death brings forgiveness. Receiving the benefits of his sacrifice means trusting him personally, not merely admiring the symbolism or knowing the story.

Jesus also directs the arrangements for the meal. The disciples find the room as he described, while Judas cannot force events beyond his control. The sermon considers the timing of the Passover and the crucifixion as evidence of God’s authority over history. Evil human intentions do not overturn his redemptive plan.

Yet this sovereign King is also a loving servant. He longs to share the meal with his disciples and stoops to wash their feet. His authority should therefore deepen our confidence in his care, not make him seem distant. We are invited to respond with thankful obedience and to come to Christ for forgiveness rather than waiting until we consider ourselves worthy.

sermons.title: The Cost of Being a Disciple
sermons.summary:
Beginning a series on discipleship, the preacher asks what a healthy follower of Jesus looks like. From Matthew 16:24, he argues that church programs, attendance and knowledge alone cannot define discipleship. Jesus speaks to those who are already his disciples, so denying oneself and carrying a cross are not fees that purchase forgiveness. The preacher first stresses the purpose of following: those saved by grace continue coming to Christ because they find rest, nourishment and joy in him. He contrasts that lasting satisfaction with a desire for an easy life that treats Jesus as a small addition to other pursuits.

The sermon then explores the three demands of the verse: deny oneself, take up one's cross and follow Jesus. Denying oneself means refusing self-rule rather than merely giving up a treat. Taking up the cross means willingness to bear shame, rejection or persecution for Christ, not simply naming every ordinary hardship a cross. Following him is an ongoing response that reaches everyday decisions, including work and leisure, without declaring those activities wrong in themselves. The preacher admits believers will stumble and calls them back to repentance and Christ's strength rather than pretending at instant perfection. He invites listeners to yield their lives willingly to the Savior who gave himself for them.

sermons.title: The Hot Jealousy of God
sermons.summary:
How can believers resist becoming absorbed in comfort and temporary pursuits? Beginning with Exodus 34:14, this sermon explores God’s jealousy as a motive for wholehearted devotion. The preacher distinguishes it from insecure, possessive human jealousy and describes it as an intense commitment to an exclusive relationship. The message asks listeners to consider not only what they avoid, but what their hearts actively pursue.

Three aspects guide the sermon: God’s jealousy for his glory, for his Son and for his people. His glory is presented as displayed through Christ, not in competition with him. The preacher connects the uniqueness of salvation in Jesus with the Father’s purpose to honour the Son. In addressing believers, he distinguishes God’s unchanging jealousy from condemnation, emphasising Christ’s bearing of wrath on behalf of the redeemed.

The final section considers the privileges and responsibilities of belonging to God. His love, faithfulness and devotion call forth grateful love and faithfulness in return. This response is not presented as earning salvation or claiming present sinless perfection. Listeners are urged to confess rival attachments, follow Christ and move beyond minimum compliance. A searching practical question closes the message: does a chosen pursuit help deepen love for Christ, or draw the heart away from him?

sermons.title: The Manifold Mercies of God
sermons.summary:
The sermon explores the manifold mercy of God as the attribute that makes a holy God approachable to broken sinners. Mercy is God’s tender, compassionate care for people ruined by sin. His general mercy reaches across creation: he restrains judgment, shows patience, warns sinners, and gives them time to turn to Christ. This kindness must not be treated as permission to continue in sin, because the opportunity to receive mercy in this life will not last forever.

God’s sovereign mercy is his saving compassion toward his people. It is not grounded in righteous deeds or personal sorrow, but in God’s own freedom and loving purpose. The message describes this mercy as salvific, undeserved, great, and parental. It rescued violent opponents such as Paul, continues to care for believers who stumble, and sometimes disciplines them rather than abandoning them. Because God is rich in mercy, his children should run toward him when guilty instead of hiding as though he were reluctant to receive them. The cross displays the depth of his compassion and assures sinners that abundant mercy is found in Jesus. Unbelievers are urged to seek that mercy while there is opportunity; believers are called to enjoy it, praise God for it, and extend mercy to others rather than hoarding what they have received.

sermons.title: Christ-Centered Slaves
sermons.summary:
Working through Colossians 3:22–4:1, this sermon examines first-century slavery and uses it to explain wholehearted devotion to Jesus Christ. It distinguishes Roman slavery from modern employment and notes that ancient slaves could enter bondage through war, birth, or debt, performed many kinds of work, and belonged legally to their masters. Their welfare depended greatly on a master’s character. The sermon does not treat criminal exploitation as acceptable. Instead, it focuses on how the New Testament’s master-slave imagery portrays the Christian’s relationship to Christ.

Believers were once enslaved to sin but have been purchased by Jesus’ blood and now belong exclusively to him. This identity calls for complete obedience rather than selective compliance, and sincere service rather than outward performance designed to impress people. Christ’s followers should not do the minimum, reserve uncommanded areas for self-rule, or serve only when convenient. Their controlling purpose is to please the Master who owns them, using time, possessions, energy, and every decision for his glory. The sermon also points to Christ’s promised reward for faithful service and warns that wrongdoing has consequences without partiality. Its appeal is to reject a diluted Christianity limited to occasional worship or personal benefit and embrace joyful dependence, wholehearted obedience, and lifelong devotion to the Lord who loved and redeemed his people.

sermons.title: A Call For Unity In The Church
sermons.summary:
Church unity requires more than shared interests, sound words, or occupying the same room. In Philippians 2:1–4, Paul calls believers to a common life shaped by humility, practical love, and concern for one another. The sermon explores the motivation, qualities, and practical pursuit of that unity, showing how selfishness can disrupt even a healthy congregation.

The encouragement found in Christ, the comfort of his love, fellowship in the Spirit, and his compassion give believers reason and strength to serve together. Being of one mind does not mean having identical tastes or lifestyles; it means sharing a Christ-centred attitude and purpose. Love must become visible through presence, care, and sacrifice, not remain a claim made from a distance.

Selfish ambition and the desire for recognition turn attention inward, even during acts of service. Humility instead regards others as important and uses personal abilities for their good. Jesus' self-giving obedience provides the pattern for this costly change of heart. Listeners are invited to examine resentment, their willingness to serve without praise, and whether they allow others to come alongside them. Growing together calls for forgiveness, patient encouragement, and a deliberate commitment to put the good of the church ahead of personal acclaim.

sermons.title: Introduction to Colossians
sermons.summary:
Colossians presents Jesus Christ as supreme and completely sufficient. Its opening identifies Paul as Christ’s authorised apostle, Timothy as his trusted companion, and the recipients as saints and faithful brothers and sisters in Christ. A saint is not an exceptional religious hero but every believer whom Christ has purchased and set apart for God. These believers belonged to a particular local church where they could love, serve and obey the Bible’s commands toward one another.

The historical setting explains why this emphasis mattered. The young church at Colossae faced a mixture of Gnostic speculation and Jewish legalism. One offered acceptance with God through Christ plus special knowledge and angel worship; the other through Christ plus ceremonial works. Both diminished Christ by implying that his person and saving work were insufficient.

Paul answers these errors by directing attention back to Christ. All wisdom and knowledge are found in him; the fullness of deity dwells in him; he rules every authority; and redemption and forgiveness are found in him. Nothing can be added to Jesus as the basis of acceptance with God. Listeners are encouraged to let this enlarged vision of Christ shape their worship and obedience, resist teaching that supplements his finished work, and live as people who belong wholly to him within a faithful local church.

sermons.title: The Beginning Of The End
sermons.summary:
The temple's impressive appearance could not overturn Jesus' declaration that it would be destroyed. Opening the study of Mark 13:1–4, the preacher contrasts the disciples' admiration for the building with Christ's judgment upon a religious system that had lost sight of him. The warning reaches beyond architecture: the activity and outward splendour of worship cannot replace trust in the one being worshipped.

The sermon distinguishes a near fulfilment in the temple's destruction from a farther fulfilment concerning Christ's coming and the end of the age. The preacher explains that distinction through the disciples' questions, the parallel account in Matthew and the scale of the events described later in Mark. He argues for a future fulfilment of those events and presents God's sovereign faithfulness as the reason his promises can be trusted. These are not offered merely as interesting predictions, but as truths intended to shape present obedience.

Christ's final victory gives believers hope amid pressure and suffering. The practical call is to loosen attachment to a world that will not last, encourage one another and give greater weight to what endures. The message closes with an urgent invitation to those who do not yet know Jesus: seek the forgiveness and refuge he freely offers now, rather than meet the coming King unprepared.

sermons.title: Living Out Our Devotion to God
sermons.summary:
Romans 12:2 explains how believers live out the dedication described in the previous verse. A once-for-all commitment to present the body to God is followed by two continuing commands: do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed through the renewing of the mind. The world presses people into its patterns, values, ambitions, and assumptions. Even activities that are not plainly sinful can weaken devotion when they feed materialism, sensuality, violence, wasted time, or the desire for approval. Christians are called to resist whatever shapes their lives contrary to the new heart God has given them.

Resistance alone is not enough. Lasting change comes as the Holy Spirit transforms believers while they deliberately fill their minds with the truth and glory of Christ in Scripture. This renewal changes desires, speech, choices, and character. It also enables Christians to experience God’s will as good, pleasing, and perfect rather than as a burden. The sermon describes people as pleasure seekers and urges them not merely to suppress worldly desires, but to seek satisfaction in Christ. Security is found in his faithful care, honour in exalting him, and justice in his righteous rule. By turning from the world and beholding Jesus, believers can remain devoted under pressure, obey from the heart, and follow Christ even when faithfulness is costly.

sermons.title: Sacrificial Worship And Church Life Are Inseparable
sermons.summary:
Christian devotion is not a solitary project. Romans 12:3–5 connects offering ourselves to God with a humble, interdependent life in the church. Christ’s people are called not only to serve one another, but also to receive the help that he supplies through other members. A profession of dependence on Jesus must not become an excuse for rejecting the means he gives for spiritual growth.

The message develops two responses: honest self-assessment and faithful cooperation. Pride can appear in chasing another person’s prominent role, despising an unnoticed gift, displaying genuine abilities for praise, or refusing counsel and encouragement. Humility neither exaggerates nor denies what God has given. Because every ability is received by grace, the appropriate response is gratitude and useful service rather than rivalry or self-promotion.

Paul’s picture of one body explains why mutual ministry matters. Different members contribute to the health of the whole, sharing suffering, encouragement and growth in the knowledge of Christ. Teaching, correction, practical help and comfort are not optional additions to an otherwise self-sufficient faith. Listeners are invited to recognise their need, welcome the gifts of fellow believers and repent of the pride that keeps others at a distance. The church’s shared life makes care for Christ’s people an everyday expression of worship.

sermons.title: The Persistent Servant
sermons.summary:
Timothy provides a living example of the humble, selfless service taught throughout Philippians 2. After ten years alongside Paul, he remained available, teachable and ready to undertake a demanding journey for the Philippian church. Paul hoped in the Lord while making his plans, trusting Christ with his imprisonment and future rather than treating circumstances as his ultimate authority.

Paul commends Timothy as a servant of kindred spirit who was genuinely concerned for the believers’ welfare. Timothy had absorbed Paul’s teaching and shared his affection, gospel convictions and desire to put others first. His concern was sincere rather than performed for appearance, and it contrasted with people who pursued their own interests. Their relationship also shows that Christian discipleship and encouragement are shared work: Timothy learned from Paul, became like him and strengthened him in return.

Timothy’s worth had been proved through years of pressure, service and hardship. Like gold tested by fire, his character had matured while he served with Paul for the advance of the gospel. The church is therefore encouraged to build relationships that form dependable servants, not passive spectators. Believers should ask whether they are available, teachable, concerned for others and willing to endure inconvenience for Christ. Mature disciples also help others grow, support their leaders and seek the church’s spiritual welfare above personal comfort or ambition.

sermons.title: Using Your Spiritual Gifts Is Not an Option | Wesam Saad
sermons.summary:
This sermon argues that serving the local church through spiritual gifts is not optional for a Christian who wants to glorify God. Holiness is not an isolated project limited to avoiding obvious sins. New Testament commands and the fruit of the Spirit are worked out in relationships within Christ’s body. Because believers love Christ, they also love the people in whom He dwells, and serving even the least of His disciples is service offered to Him. Genuine commitment to a church must therefore become active, loving, and sacrificial.

Spiritual gifts are supernatural capacities received at conversion, distinct from natural talents, and every believer receives a unique measure and combination. First Peter 4 commands each person to employ that gift in serving others. Ephesians 4 adds that these gifts equip the saints and build the body toward maturity in Christ. The sermon pictures the church as both a hospital, where every member helps care for spiritually weak people, and a body that grows only as every part works properly. Ignoring a gift harms both the member and the people who need that service. Believers are encouraged to discover and exercise the gifts God has assigned without envy, pride, or a desire for prominence. Their identity rests in the Giver, and their prayer should be, “Use me Your way.”

sermons.title: Jesus, The Chief Cornerstone | Mark 12:10-11 Part 1
sermons.summary:
The stone rejected by the builders becomes the essential reference point for the whole building. Focusing on Mark 12:10, the sermon presents Jesus as the chief cornerstone: the Saviour opposed by religious leaders yet exalted by God. Those entrusted with teaching Scripture failed to recognise the One to whom it pointed, rejecting him when his truth exposed their desires and self-reliance.

A cornerstone determines the alignment of everything built around it. The message develops that picture through Christ's supremacy over wisdom, rulers, time, mercy and the church. He is not an optional addition to a religious life. All things depend on him, and the church belongs to him as one people whose unity rests in his saving work rather than social or ethnic distinctions. His rejection does not lessen his authority or remove the seriousness of refusing him.

The application asks whether Jesus truly shapes each part of life. Measuring righteousness against him leaves no room for superiority over others. Receiving correction becomes an opportunity to seek his transforming grace. Church fellowship and family relationships should reflect his self-giving love rather than personal comfort. The closing invitation turns away from attempts to earn heaven through good works and towards the forgiveness and righteousness offered through Christ's death and resurrection.

sermons.title: Aristarchus The Encouraging Minister
sermons.summary:
Colossians 4:10 names Aristarchus as Paul’s fellow prisoner and one of the servants who proved to be an encouragement. His story begins in Thessalonica, where he believed the gospel despite strong resistance from much of the surrounding Jewish community. His conversion encouraged Paul because it demonstrated that God’s power could overcome cultural pressure and hostility. Aristarchus chose Christ even when association with the gospel exposed him to rejection, and his example encourages believers not to assume that resistant families or communities are beyond God’s saving reach.

Aristarchus continued to encourage Paul through costly companionship. He was seized during the riot in Ephesus, travelled with Paul while knowing that affliction awaited, endured the dangerous journey and shipwreck toward Rome, and then voluntarily remained with Paul in imprisonment. The sermon draws three lessons from this steadfast ministry. An encourager reminds suffering believers of Christ and helps them keep running the race. An encourager also shares life deeply, bearing pain and rejoicing together rather than offering only inexpensive words. Finally, an encourager serves humbly, often in the background, so others are freed to carry out their calling. Believers are invited to seek hurting brothers and sisters, stay beside them through difficulty, share their burdens, and serve without competition so that Christ is honored and the gospel advances.

sermons.title: Use Your Spiritual Gifts
sermons.summary:
God gives spiritual gifts to strengthen the church, not to provide a private source of importance or fascination. In Romans 12:6–8, the call to use these gifts grows out of a life offered to God and transformed through Christ. Believers need one another: humility recognises that growth cannot happen in isolation, while love turns the gifts received into practical service.

The message concentrates on preaching, serving and teaching. Preaching must faithfully communicate the written Word, addressing understanding, affections and obedience rather than simply entertaining an audience. Its authority is measured by the faith delivered in Scripture, not the preacher’s confidence or popularity. Practical service includes ordinary acts of care and should be wholehearted, even when inconvenient or costly. Teaching explains truth clearly and patiently so that people understand it and can respond obediently. These gifts differ and overlap, but share the purpose of building up Christ’s body.

Listeners are encouraged to use what God has actually given them without coveting another role or delaying service until their gifts are precisely classified. Those who speak should welcome counsel, prepare carefully, repent of known sin and depend on Christ. Neither unrepentance nor a demand for personal perfection is a sound foundation for ministry. The immediate response is to begin serving faithfully with the abilities and opportunities already available.

sermons.title: Jesus Is The God-Man
sermons.summary:
Knowing religious truths is not the same as knowing the Saviour they reveal. In Mark 12:35–37, Jesus challenges an incomplete understanding of the Messiah by asking how David can call his own descendant Lord. The question takes listeners beyond admiration for a human king towards the identity of Jesus as both truly human and truly God.

The sermon first explains Christ's role as the promised deliverer from sin and its destructive consequences. His descent from David fulfils the expectation of a human king, but that truth must not become a limit on who he is. Drawing on Psalm 110, the message presents David's Lord as sharing divine authority and reigning over his enemies. Jesus' humanity enables him to represent his people, while his divine power grounds their confidence in his saving work.

This teaching also reveals mercy. Jesus addresses hostile religious leaders with questions intended to bring them to recognise and embrace him. Listeners are challenged to let Scripture shape their understanding of Christ rather than selecting only what suits their hopes. Salvation rests in Jesus himself, not in religious standing or confidence in one's own faith. His humility in bearing sin calls for wholehearted trust, worship and satisfaction in him.

sermons.title: Rescued From Darkness Into Light
sermons.summary:
Colossians 1:13 gives believers a reason for gratitude: the Father has rescued them from the power of darkness and transferred them into the kingdom of his beloved Son. The sermon describes darkness as Satan’s deceptive influence over the world. It blinds minds to Christ, captures affections with lesser pleasures, and leaves people confused, fearful, and unable to free themselves. Respectability or order does not remove this bondage, because its effect is spiritual blindness to the light of the gospel.

God’s rescue comes through Jesus Christ, the King who entered life, defeated temptation, and triumphed through the cross. His death broke the devil’s claim and freed believers from slavery to the fear of death. Yet salvation is more than release from captivity. The Father has already brought his people into Christ’s kingdom—a realm of righteousness, peace, joy, truth, and order. Jesus rules with power and love, joins his people to himself, strengthens them in weakness, and keeps them under his care. The sermon therefore calls Christians to resist being governed by feelings during trials, remember God’s blessings, and cultivate thankful joy. Their lives should agree with their words by pursuing Christ as their greatest delight. Those still in darkness are urged to seek mercy from Jesus, the only Saviour able to rescue them and bring them into his kingdom.

sermons.title: The Proof of The Resurrection
sermons.summary:
Jesus Christ’s bodily resurrection is the foundation of Christian hope and God’s public affirmation of his work on the cross. If Christ had remained in the grave, preaching and faith would be empty and sin would remain unforgiven. Mark’s final resurrection account instead presents a risen Lord whose victory secures eternal life and demands a response.

Jesus truly died and was buried, witnessed by Roman soldiers, members of the Jewish council, the crowd and his followers. The tomb was genuinely empty, as even the authorities’ attempt to explain the missing body effectively acknowledged. Women, disciples, guards and angels encountered the evidence, while the grave clothes remained behind. Jesus then appeared alive to his disciples and hundreds of others, speaking and eating with them. Their transformation from fearful followers into bold witnesses willing to suffer for what they had seen adds further weight.

This is not a call to blind or irrational belief, but to consider the testimony and its implications. The risen Jesus is Lord, will return and offers salvation to those who trust him. For believers, his resurrection promises a future bodily resurrection and removes the enslaving fear of death. They are urged to remain steadfast, invest their short lives in the Lord’s work and let eternity reshape their priorities, knowing that faithful labour in Christ is not wasted.

sermons.title: The Peacemaking Christian
sermons.summary:
Paul’s appeal to Euodia and Syntyche in Philippians 4 shows why peace within the church matters. These women were genuine believers and active gospel workers, yet conflict had disrupted their harmony. Paul addresses both without taking sides and urges them to agree in the Lord. His loving directness shows that ignoring a quarrel is not kindness: unresolved strife can grow, draw others into opposing camps, and weaken the whole church. Christian unity is not built merely on shared interests or personalities, but on Christ, the gospel, and the heavenly hope believers hold together.

The sermon therefore calls Christians to address conflict promptly and humbly. Each person should seek reconciliation without hiding behind who started the dispute, remaining teachable when another believer offers help. Paul also calls a trusted companion to help the women, reminding the church that peacemaking is a shared responsibility carried out gently, without gossip or favouritism. Believers are encouraged to examine whether they solve problems or create them, to receive wise help when needed, and to remember the grace Christ has shown them. Those who are not reconciled to God are urged first to turn to Jesus in repentance and faith. The church honours Christ as its members pursue peace, bear one another’s burdens, and keep striving together for the gospel.

sermons.title: The All sufficiency of God | Wes Saad
sermons.summary:
God is entirely self-sufficient: he depends on no creature for life, happiness, wisdom, strength or the fulfilment of his purposes. Unlike idols that must be made, decorated, carried and defended, the living God possesses life in himself and gives life to everything else. Human faith does not increase his glory, and human rejection cannot diminish him. This truth humbles every claim that God needs our talent, money or ministry.

The other side of this truth is our complete dependence on him. Every breath and every good gift comes from God, yet people abandon the fountain of living water and seek satisfaction in relationships, possessions, achievement or personal independence. Those created things cannot meet the soul’s deepest hunger. God alone can satisfy it through Jesus Christ.

Why, then, do people serve a God who lacks nothing? Not to supply a deficiency in him, but to receive his grace and display his sufficiency. Obedience, ministry and generosity glorify God when they show that he—not success or comfort—is the believer’s treasure. Trials expose false sources of satisfaction and teach reliance on Christ’s sufficient grace, as Paul learned through his weakness. Believers are encouraged to seek God earnestly, abandon rival pleasures and respond to suffering with heartfelt obedience, endurance and joy so the world can see that he truly is enough.

sermons.title: Rejoicing in Suffering
sermons.summary:
In Colossians 1:24–25, Paul says that he rejoices in his sufferings for the church. This is not denial, forced optimism, or delight in pain. Paul knows grief and anguish, yet beneath them is a durable joy rooted beyond the rewards of this world. Imprisonment, rejection, physical hardship, and false accusation do not control him because his treasure, identity, and purpose are anchored in Christ and his coming kingdom. Suffering for Jesus also confirms that Paul belongs to the Master who was rejected before him, making hardship an honoured participation in Christ’s cause rather than evidence that God has forgotten him.

Paul’s afflictions do not add anything to Christ’s saving work. They accompany the spreading of that salvation through the preaching of the gospel. He endures them for Christ’s body, the church, loving both its Head and its members and standing for their freedom in Jesus. His willingness to suffer strengthens the credibility of the truth he teaches. Rejoicing in hardship also makes witness powerful: observers see a hope that loss cannot destroy. The sermon calls believers to serve the church without demanding repayment, continue speaking of Christ when rejected, and let suffering expose pride and deepen dependence on Jesus. As God meets them with grace, their joy can point others to the strength and worth of their Saviour.

sermons.title: Authority Over Sin
sermons.summary:
A crowded house becomes the setting for an extraordinary declaration: Jesus tells a paralysed man that his sins are forgiven. This sermon on Luke 5:15–20 follows the scene through the critics, the carriers and Christ. Before entering the house, it notices Jesus withdrawing to pray even as his popularity grows, modelling dependence on the Father rather than the approval of a crowd.

The religious critics provide a warning about approaching God’s word with self-satisfaction instead of need. The men carrying their helpless companion display a contrasting posture. When the crowd blocks their way, they bring him through the roof, determined to place him before Jesus. The preacher sees sacrificial love and confidence in Christ expressed through their persistence, and asks whether listeners discourage such service or willingly share its cost.

Jesus addresses the man’s deepest need with forgiveness. The sermon emphasises the compassion, grace and completeness of his response: he welcomes the needy person rather than demanding that he first establish his worthiness. The closing application calls believers to put aside self-righteousness, come to Christ honestly and help others approach him. This includes both people who need to hear the gospel and fellow believers weighed down by guilt or discouragement. The remainder of the narrative is reserved for a later message.

sermons.title: A Living Hope for Living Stones
sermons.summary:
In this sermon on 1 Peter 2, the preacher uses the building of a house to explain why its foundation matters. He presents Jesus as the living, chosen and precious cornerstone of God's spiritual house. Without him, he says, the church cannot stand firm through the trials and persecution Peter addresses. Coming to Christ begins with repentance and faith, but the preacher also urges believers to keep drawing near to him for refuge, strength and fellowship. He asks listeners not to settle for outward religious activity while remaining apart from the one on whom the whole building depends.

The preacher then describes believers as living stones whom God is fitting together, rather than isolated bricks. Their shared life is meant to reflect their builder and to encourage one another amid suffering. Peter's image of a holy priesthood leads him to explain that Christ has opened access to God and that believers now offer spiritual sacrifices through him. He names the practical service of one's whole life, praise, doing good, sharing, witness and prayer. These are not substitutes for Christ's foundation, but ways of serving upon it. The sermon closes by urging gratitude, reverence and useful participation in the church, while inviting unbelieving listeners to rest on Christ rather than their own works.

sermons.title: God Hates Divorce
sermons.summary: This sermon continues a verse-by-verse exposition of Mark 10:1-9 and asks why God hates divorce. It begins by presenting marriage as a portrait of Christ's relationship with the church: the husband and wife are called to display that union rather than treat marriage mainly as a path to personal happiness. The sermon explains the Pharisees' question about divorce as a hostile attempt to trap Jesus in a setting associated with John the Baptist's confrontation with Herod. Jesus responds by directing them away from what Moses permitted and toward what God commands. The message then follows Jesus back to creation, arguing that God made man and woman for marriage, gives a spouse as a gift, forms the one-flesh bond, and is himself the one who joins a husband and wife. Because the bond is God's work, the sermon urges faithfulness even when marriage brings loneliness or suffering. It warns against expecting a spouse to provide ultimate satisfaction and points instead to the sufficiency of Christ. The closing appeal calls listeners to confess selfishness and unfaithfulness, receive forgiveness through Jesus' death, trust him alone, and seek strength to honour God in married life. Every statement remains a private draft requiring administrator review of the retained captions, Scripture references, and pastoral claims.

sermons.title: The Compassionate Christian
sermons.summary:
Paul’s appeal to “stand firm in the Lord” is surrounded by warm affection for the Philippian church. Before giving the command, he calls them his beloved brethren, says he longs to see them, and names them his joy and crown. The sermon presents this as a model of compassionate Christian encouragement. Paul does not motivate people through threats, irritation, or self-importance. Though he is an apostle, he approaches them first as a humble brother whose unconditional love reflects the Father’s love for the Son and Christ’s love for his church. His desire is not distant goodwill but fellowship and their growth toward the heavenly city.

This affection gives strength to the command. Standing firm is a continuing, active responsibility for every believer, like soldiers holding their position together under attack. Yet it can be done only “in the Lord,” abiding in Christ and relying on the strength he supplies. The church protects and encourages one another when its members value fellow believers above status, comfort, possessions, or achievement. The sermon asks what believers count as their joy and crown, whether they long for fellowship, and how they serve the local body in deeds as well as words. Against a self-centred culture, Christians are called to love patiently, humbly, and sacrificially so they can run together for the gospel.

sermons.title: What Man Despises, God Honours
sermons.summary:
The mockery surrounding Jesus’ crucifixion reveals a sharp difference between human judgments and God’s purposes. Where onlookers see weakness and disgrace, the cross displays divine sovereignty, the compassion of Christ and the seriousness of unbelief. The suffering of Jesus is not an unforeseen defeat. Even hostile actions serve a purpose that his enemies neither understand nor intend, giving believers reason to trust God amid their own trials.

Jesus identifies with condemned sinners rather than protecting his reputation among the powerful. His place between criminals expresses the mercy of a King who comes to rescue the guilty. Remaining on the cross is not a failure of strength: his love and his work as a substitute keep him there. Saving others means bearing the judgment from which they need deliverance. The mockers’ accusation therefore points, unintentionally, towards the heart of his saving work.

Unbelief interprets these events wrongly and demands another sign while resisting what God has already made known. Listeners are urged to receive his word rather than make faith depend on spectacle. For believers, the cross also changes the measure of greatness. Wealth, status and comfort give way to sacrificial love, compassion for sinners and willingness to bear Christ’s reproach while seeking the lasting future he promises.

sermons.title: Faith Wrapped in Love 1 | Peter 1:8
sermons.summary:
First Peter describes believers who love and trust Jesus although they have not seen him. This sermon explores unseen faith as encouragement and a test of genuine Christianity. Sight is insufficient to create faith: people saw Jesus’ miracles, heard him, and even touched him yet still rejected him. Biblical faith instead comes through hearing the word of Christ and is shown when believers continue loving and trusting Jesus amid persecution, sorrow, sickness, and trials. Such love is not a passing emotion, an earned exchange, or a response dependent on favourable circumstances. It is God’s work in the heart and rests on knowing who Jesus is.

The message gives reasons to love and trust Christ: he loved sinners first, gave himself for them, intercedes for his people, remains with them, supplies his Spirit, and works even suffering for their good. That trust produces inexpressible joy and an enduring, undivided love that becomes visible in ordinary relationships. Love for Jesus is expressed through patience under pressure, kindness toward difficult people, forgiveness, hospitality, service, generosity, fellowship, and care for both believers and neighbours. Listeners are urged to examine whether their love for Christ is growing, deepen it through Scripture, prayer, worship, and fellowship, and turn from competing loves. Those who do not know Christ are called to repent and come to him now.

sermons.title: Courageous for The Gospel
sermons.summary:
Using Acts 4:1–4, this sermon calls Christians to courageous gospel witness despite rejection or persecution. Peter and John proclaim that Jesus was crucified, raised from the dead, and offers forgiveness to those who repent. They speak in the temple, where religious leaders strongly oppose their message, and are arrested while still teaching. Their experience shows that visible evidence, careful explanation, or a gracious life does not guarantee acceptance. The gospel confronts self-righteousness and exclusive claims to salvation, so opposition should be expected rather than treated as proof that witness has failed.

The sermon emphasises that every Christian is called to testify about Christ, even though some may speak more publicly than others. Courage is not the absence of fear but faithful proclamation while knowing the possible cost. Peter and John continue because people cannot believe a message they never hear, and because Jesus alone saves. Their imprisonment does not prevent God from bringing many listeners to faith. Later, even after being flogged and ordered to stop, the apostles continue teaching publicly and from house to house. Believers are therefore urged not to prejudge who may respond, abandon difficult relatives or neighbours, or wait for a safer moment. They should speak truth gently but clearly, pray for hearers, and trust God to give life through the risen Christ.

sermons.title: Why Seek Heaven?
sermons.summary:
Colossians 3:3–4 gives three compelling reasons for Christians to keep seeking the things above. First, believers have died with Christ: they are no longer condemned by God’s law, ruled by worldly passions, or defined by the ambitions of this world. Second, their true life is hidden with Christ in God. Though the world may misunderstand or despise them, Christ securely holds their eternal life and is himself their present source of nourishment, satisfaction and strength. Third, Christ will return in glory, and his people will be revealed with him.

These past, present and future realities call for an energetic pursuit of heaven rather than a reluctant or divided response. The sermon urges believers to refuse pleasures and ambitions that choke their usefulness to Christ, while recognising that ordinary work, homes and possessions are not wrong in themselves. Earthly gifts should serve heavenly purposes. Christians are encouraged to delight in Christ, teach their children about him, love and serve the church, spread the gospel and endure sacrifice with confidence. The message also pleads with unbelievers not to reject Christ’s gracious offer of forgiveness and eternal life, but to come to him while there is still opportunity.

sermons.title: Luke The Faithful
sermons.summary:
Luke’s life is presented as a model of compassionate, wholehearted and faithful service to Christ. Paul calls him the beloved physician, a description that reflects more than competence. Luke cared for weak, hurting and overlooked people rather than treating ministry as a task to complete at their expense. His writings repeatedly draw attention to Christ’s compassion, and his friendship with Paul showed the same tenderness in practice. The sermon challenges believers to become people whose service reaches hearts, not merely external needs, by first dwelling on the loving character of Jesus.

Luke also placed his education, medical knowledge, careful research and writing ability at Christ’s disposal. Instead of using those gifts to magnify himself, he employed them to show the greatness of Jesus and to serve the gospel. His devotion endured through years of ministry and personal danger. When others withdrew from Paul during intense persecution, Luke remained with him, offering practical care and companionship to the end. Christians are therefore urged to dedicate every ability they possess to Christ, stand with suffering believers and serve without laziness. Faithful sacrifice is sustained by confidence that the Lord sees it and promises a lasting reward.

sermons.title: In The Presence of A Holy God
sermons.summary:
Isaiah 6:1–4 gives the church a vision of the Lord whose greatness can sustain unity among people of many backgrounds. In a year marked by a king’s death, moral decline, and national danger, Isaiah sees the King still seated on his throne. He is high and exalted, his majesty fills the temple, and no earthly change unsettles his reign. The sermon identifies this glorious Lord with Christ and urges believers to place circumstances—including trials, rulers, and uncertain futures—beneath his sovereign authority. A high view of God reshapes worship and life, drawing the church together around one supreme purpose rather than leaving fellowship as a brief weekly gathering.

The seraphim cry, “Holy, holy, holy,” declaring that God is unique and incomparable. His holiness is displayed in every attribute: he defines righteousness, possesses unmatched power, creates and sustains all things, and fills the earth with his glory. Even sinless angels cover themselves before him, yet they remain ready to serve and praise with wholehearted joy. Their worship teaches believers reverence, humility, readiness, and delight. The message calls the church to behold God as he truly is, proclaim his greatness, and put its hands together in service. As people share this vision of the holy and sovereign Lord, they find a foundation for loving unity, courageous prayer, and worship.

sermons.title: The Christ Centred Wife
sermons.summary:
This sermon considers the Christian home as a place where faith must become visible in everyday conduct. Focusing on wives in 1 Peter 3:1–6, the preacher connects Peter’s instructions with the letter’s earlier teaching about hope, holiness and Christ’s example under suffering. Church activity, he argues, must not become a reason to overlook relationships at home.

The message explains submission to one’s own husband as part of honouring Christ, including where husband and wife do not share the same faith. It expressly says that a wife must not comply with a demand to sin, and warns husbands against using the passage as a weapon against their wives. The preacher also discusses the situation in which an unbelieving spouse chooses to leave.

Attention then turns to the character of this witness: respectful conduct, inward beauty, gentleness and a quiet spirit. These are contrasted with reliance on appearance or repeated arguments, not with a blanket prohibition on attractive clothing or speaking the gospel. Sarah and the women who hoped in God provide the closing example. Listeners are urged to look to Christ, pray for their husbands and seek a transformed heart. The sermon acknowledges that faithful conduct does not guarantee a spouse’s conversion.

sermons.title: Yahweh, The Strength Of The Pilgrim
sermons.summary:
The Christian journey can be exhausting, especially when pain, opposition and ordinary burdens weaken the desire to serve. Psalm 121 is presented as encouragement for pilgrims whose destination lies beyond this world. The preacher follows two connected assurances: Yahweh is their helper in the journey and their keeper throughout it. Looking up means trusting the Creator, not expecting the mountains or another created thing to provide ultimate security.

God's power is joined to his faithful attention. The one who made and sustains all things does not grow tired of watching over his people. The promise of keeping is explained as protection from finally falling away, not a claim that believers never stumble or struggle. Likewise, the psalm's language of shelter does not promise the removal of every difficulty. God strengthens his people through suffering and preserves them on their way home.

That assurance gives a practical reason to keep loving, serving and speaking about Christ. Different believers carry different burdens, but they depend on the same faithful Lord. Rather than attempting to solve every problem before seeking help, listeners are urged to bring their weakness to him in prayer. Present trials become opportunities to grow and glorify God, while confidence rests in his preserving care rather than the traveller's own strength.

sermons.title: The Faithfulness of God | Sunday Teachings
sermons.summary:
Broken promises can leave people fearful, disappointed and unsure whom to trust. God’s faithfulness offers a different foundation: he is dependable in his character and fulfils what he has promised. The message distinguishes this assurance from expecting God to satisfy every personal desire. Trust means aligning our hopes with his word, not treating him as a servant of our preferred plans.
